This measure allows for constraints on theories beyond the Standard Model that may influence the $B^0_s$ system and was found to be 1.440 picoseconds. Additionally, a comparison was drawn with previous findings and equivalent measurements for $B^0\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decays, also incorporating updated information on $B^0_s$ and $B^0$ lifetimes. A calculation of the $C$-parity of $K^+K^-$ final states was made possible by this measurement. A search for rare $B^0_s\rightarrow \phi\phi$ decays was also conducted, with estimated branching fractions of $4.3\times10^{-6}$ and a lifetime similar to that found for $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decays. A calculation of the total decay width of $B^0_s$ mesons was then made, with a value of around 0.88 picoseconds$^{-1}$. A comparison was drawn with theoretical predictions and quantum chromodynamics calculations, with results from both approaches falling within 0.2 picoseconds$^{-1}$ of each other. This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships. Unlike conventional approaches that require adherence to these dependencies, our work aims to explore theories for handling instances that breach certain dependencies, with no preconditions on the presence of missing values. We establish a framework where each data entry can be associated with a truth status: true, false, inconsistent, or undetermined. Furthermore, our framework facilitates examination of pressing problems like data quality assessments, query validation, and data merging. Specifically, we investigate query validation as the central problem of this research, building on the foundation established by recent studies. Key contributions of this research are (a) an innovative strategy for handling inconsistencies, (b) methods for determining the truth status of queries, and (c) an examination of our approach's relevance to Four-valued logic and data merging. Additionally, we provide practical applications of our framework to real-world problems and showcase its performance on artificially generated datasets and real-life datasets. Moreover, we discuss implementation possibilities and potential extensions to our approach. Finally, we make our implementation available to the public. This research received no external funding. This study presents a novel dynamic econometric model called Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with external covariates, specifically designed to analyze and forecast count-based time series data. Our research indicates that a score-driven approach is particularly effective in capturing the evolution of time-varying parameters and allows for modeling complex dynamics and shifts within such data sets. Furthermore, we have analyzed the theoretical characteristics of the TV-PARX model, demonstrating under mild conditions that maximum likelihood estimation yields reliable and normally-distributed estimates of model parameters. To evaluate the TV-PARX model's performance and forecasting capabilities in real-world scenarios, we conducted a series of Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, we have applied the time-varying specification of the TV-PARX model to empirical data sets, analyzing new daily COVID-19 cases in Italy and corporate defaults in the US. Our findings show that the time-varying PARX model outperforms its constant-parameter counterpart across various criteria. Our research contributes to the existing literature on score-driven models by incorporating external covariates and presenting a comprehensive framework for TV-PARX models. Our research has been conducted without any external funding. Our code is publicly available online.

We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
replicates both object points and relative poses in relation to a target, using
category-level descriptors. We apply this representation in object manipulation,
with the aim of repeating tasks on new object instances from the same category
after witnessing a single demonstration. To achieve this, we use optimization
to locate the pose whose descriptor corresponds to that in the demonstration. NDFs
are efficiently trained without expert input, using a self-supervised 3D
auto-encoder, and exhibit robust performance across 6-DoF rotations and translations.
In experiments, NDFs master tasks from just a handful (5-10) demonstrations,
in both simulation and with a physical robot. Results show our method excels at
generalizing over different object instances and poses, surpassing a comparison
method relying on 2D descriptors. The NDF project is hosted at https://yilundu.github.io/ndf/.

Specifically for QCD's relevant universality classes in three dimensions, we have determined $|z_c|/R_\chi^{1/\gamma}$ to be approximately 1.607, 1.589 for $N=2, 4$ respectively. Alternatively, we have previously found $|z_c|$ to be around 2.03, 1.68 for $N=2, 4$ although these earlier results have a larger systematic uncertainty. The discovered edge singularity occurs at a critical charge that marks the onset of the vacuum's symmetry breaking in the presence of a small quark mass or similar external fields, indicating it serves as a signal for the disappearance of the trivial solution within the renormalization group flow. By leveraging wide-field photometry through telescopic observations, we can gather data from numerous stars simultaneously, over extended periods, and under nearly all weather conditions, save for extreme cloud cover. Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed. The first segment employs CNN outputs directly for final task estimation, whereas in the second segment, intermediate cues derived from CNNs are utilized to achieve the desired outcome. This study focuses on the latter category by employing two crucial techniques. Firstly, we modify the projection of a 3D object onto an image to create a projection that closely resembles the actual image, thereby reducing the dimensional space for pose estimation. Secondly, we introduce a novel method called projection grouping, where multiple projections from diverse viewing angles are combined to determine a pose. This approach leverages the inherent properties of high-dimensional spaces to enhance estimation accuracy. Furthermore, we explore the integration of correspondence learning into the framework to enhance pose estimation accuracy. Experimental results validate the effectiveness of our approach, demonstrating superior performance compared to existing methods across five challenging datasets. Numerous numerical methods for resolving stochastic differential equations in molecular dynamics simulations have been proposed, and we have discovered their limitations to be particularly relevant for our purposes. By leveraging the deterministic and stochastic components of differential equation solvers, we have established a framework that enables us to accurately determine configuration sampling efficiencies and biases. This framework comprises two distinct components: (1) a performance metric that evaluates the efficiency of configurational sampling based on the variance of the solvers' deterministic components, and (2) a detection method for bias in configurational sampling caused by the solvers' stochastic components. To validate our framework, we conducted comprehensive simulations of ligand-receptor interactions and found that using the optimal solver resulted in enhanced performance, with a 10-fold increase in computational speed possible for certain systems. In addition, our research demonstrated that the Langevin Dynamics solver exhibits minimal stochastic bias, whereas the Velocity Verlet solver exhibits more pronounced stochastic bias, with the Langevin Impulse solver displaying intermediate behavior. Nonetheless, the Langevin Dynamics solver was found to demonstrate deterministically extraneous configurational sampling, and by modifying the solver, we were able to rectify this issue. As a result, we are able to publicly disseminate the improved solver, known as the Langevin Impulse solver, in the hope that it will be beneficial to the molecular dynamics community. Moreover, the research outcomes are visualized in an appendix. The Langevin Impulse solver code is also provided. Our new method calculates a variation of eigenvector centrality for multi-layered networks that incorporate node importance across different layers. In these networks, defined by separate interconnected graphs without connections between different layers, the value of a node's centrality is determined by the sum of the values of the connected nodes within each specific layer, similar to traditional eigenvector centrality calculations. Unlike standard approaches, our approach takes into account the relationships between different network layers and their respective impact on the centrality values. Unlike current multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks that account for inter-layer connections, our approach uses a separate set of equations that can be solved using a hybrid algorithm. This algorithm first determines the centrality values for a temporary set of equation solutions, followed by a correction phase that aligns the solutions with the desired equation format. We validate our method by applying it to synthetic and real-world datasets, including Facebook's collaboration networks and international air transportation routes. Our results show that this method outperforms current multi-layer eigenvector centrality approaches in terms of centrality distribution accuracy. We also explore different model variations and discuss the method's limitations. Further analysis reveals that our approach can be viewed as a variation of the current weighted betweenness centrality for multi-layer networks. Finally, we provide the algorithm's source code for public use. Our research also identifies several potential research directions. This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal that occurs as the sphere enters the water's surface. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. In fact, at mid-range speeds, pinch-off times relate differently to fluid dynamics than they do at either low or high speeds, indicating that increased pressures inside the formed cavity play a significant role. In addition, our findings include the shift from the deeper water-entrapment phenomenon to the surface-seal regime, and observations on the partial-seal, rippling-cavity-surface, and secondary pinch-off stages of water-entry interactions. Understanding these stages is crucial for better modeling such interactions. A comprehensive discussion of previous and current research is also presented. Our data further highlight the importance of correctly accounting for the pressures within the formed cavity when analyzing water-entry interactions, and we propose a more comprehensive framework for this purpose. A well-known hypothesis posits that gravity at a quantum level must be devoid of universal symmetries. A burgeoning field in quantum physics, known as multi-phonon physics, is driving research and development for both fundamental understanding and applications in metrology and communication systems. Quantum acoustic resonators serve as the ideal testing ground for multi-phonon phenomena through a combination of theoretical and experimental studies. The specific system studied consists of a semiconductor quantum dot driven by a laser, coupled to an acoustic cavity, and has exhibited remarkable multi-phonon properties, including the generation of non-classical acoustic fields, and the achievement of quantum entanglement between acoustic modes and electron spins. The research also explored the fundamental principles of this system by developing a generalized theoretical framework based on the quantum Rabi model, and identified the conditions necessary to create multi-phonon states in both theoretical and real-world implementations. Furthermore, the replacement of the quantum dot with a 2D semiconductor layer, and the use of external magnetic fields, were proposed as potential means of enhancing the multi-phonon effects and transitioning from the quantum regime to classical thermodynamic behavior. The study has the potential to translate theoretical advancements into real-world applications, and could be experimentally verified in 2D semiconductor layers with a strong electron spin phonon coupling. The research also highlighted the dark states and oscillations that can be created and manipulated, and the resulting knowledge can be combined with 2D semiconductor layers, with or without external magnetic fields, to create novel quantum acoustic effects based on the quantum dot's electron spin. The corresponding proposals for experimental verification include using microcavities with a dot or a 2D layer at the center, and could also be extended to other systems, such as microresonators, by replacing the quantum dot with a 2D layer mounted on one of the resonator's ends. The research provides the theoretical foundation for the experimental verification of dark states and the corresponding phonon oscillations in various systems. The study of open systems is also discussed, and the resulting knowledge can be combined with 2D semiconductor layers, with or without external magnetic fields, to create novel quantum acoustic effects based on the quantum dot's electron spin. Quantum states known as single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be generated via quantum-optical catalysis using beam splitters or parametric amplifiers. These states occur when a coherent state and a single-photon state interact in two input ports, and a photon is detected in a specific output channel. We examine the success probabilities associated with detecting these states, as they vary depending on the catalytic device used. Notably, our analysis reveals that states produced by beam splitters and parametric amplifiers exhibit the same characteristics when analyzing the distribution of photons. We thoroughly investigate the unique quantum properties of SPCCSs, including sub-Poisson statistics, anti-bunching effects, and quadrature squeezing. These findings demonstrate that SPCCSs possess abundant non-classical behavior, thereby conferring a quantum advantage for executing various technological tasks. We also explore the relationship between SPCCSs and other renowned quantum states, revealing that they can be created under the same conditions as other states, such as single-photon catalyzed Glauber states, N-photon catalyzed coherent states, or even Schrödinger cat states, depending on the optical device used. Ultimately, our research highlights the versatility of quantum-optical catalysis in generating diverse non-classical states via a single setup. The corresponding quantum circuit is incredibly straightforward and requires minimal quantum components, primarily including a beam splitter or a parametric amplifier as the core device. We outline our approach to evaluating the quantum properties of SPCCSs in both the phase-space Schrödinger picture and the Wigner function picture, which provides a more visual representation of these properties. The resulting anti-bunching spectra and quadrature squeezing spectra can be used as indicators of the non-classical behavior exhibited by SPCCSs. The amount of quadrature squeezing increases as the coherent state's amplitude decreases, ultimately reaching infinite squeezing when the state transitions to a single-photon state. Notably, the amount of squeezing remains bounded for states generated by beam splitters. This review focuses on explaining the fundamental principles and detailed calculations of bivectors within the Newman-Penrose formalism, specifically by converting a complex self-dual electromagnetic field from the standard Minkowski space basis to the complex null tetrad basis. As a result, we derive the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor in the context of Newman-Penrose formalism. Furthermore, this process is illustrated through two approaches: directly converting the electromagnetic field's basis, and alternatively, by analyzing the complex coefficient equations in the Newman-Penrose formalism. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive overview of the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor in the Newman-Penrose formalism, concluding that this formalism offers a straightforward and intuitive understanding of the complex coefficients and their relationships. Lastly, this review is concluded by examining the relationship between the Newman-Penrose complex coefficients and the electromagnetic field's basis, which involves a transformation of the bivectors. A recent framework combining artificial neural networks and mixed integer linear programming for designing chemical compounds has been built upon to create a new method for polymer inference. This new method incorporates a unique way of depicting polymers using monomers, new descriptors that capture their structure, and employs linear regression in the predictive framework. Computational trials have demonstrated that the proposed approach excels in predicting specific chemical properties in polymers, also successfully modeling compounds composed of up to 50 non-hydrogen atoms within a monomeric structure. Furthermore, this method has been found to outperform the current state-of-the-art paradigm based on graph neural networks in predicting the melting point of polyesters composed of up to 20 atom types. Additionally, the proposed framework has been applied to a real-world problem of inferring polymers from experimental data, yielding promising results. The code for this project is available online at https://github.com/wenhao-liang/Polymers-IP.

Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we developed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This model leverages spatial and channel attention mechanisms in dense blocks to prioritize specific features and regions. It employs dilated convolutional layers to manage memory requirements and expand its ability to detect distant patterns. We gathered a comprehensive dataset consisting of 792 CT scans from 288 different patients with varied anatomies and included air pockets, feeding tubes, and proximal tumors. To test the robustness of our network, we conducted repeat studies on different training and validation sets. Our model produced a dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.79, a mean surface distance of 5.4 mm, and a Hausdorff distance of 14.7 mm for 287 test scans. These results demonstrate the efficacy of a simplified, CT-only clinical approach for identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus. Our code is available online at this link https://github.com/yousefis/DenseUnet_Esophagus_Segmentation. Moreover, we created a detailed guide to replicate our dataset, available at this link https://github.com/yousefis/Esophagus_Segmentation_Dataset. Lastly, we contributed a feature extraction technique using transfer learning, which can be found at this link https://github.com/yousefis/Esophagus_Segmentation_Features. Human-generated descriptions are commonly used to train and evaluate image description systems, which are typically ranked based on their similarity to these descriptions. This method's reliability hinges on the quality of these descriptions. Since, as demonstrated in Section 2, current datasets are inadequate, I believe we require more precise guidelines balancing visually impaired users' needs and practical description generation feasibility. High-quality reference data could be ideal for system evaluation, yet we must also consider other alternatives. I outline specific issues with various description quality assessment metrics and propose a straightforward, practical method using a survey-based tool to assess descriptions in existing datasets. Additionally, I discuss the challenges of acquiring new, high-quality reference data and present possible avenues for their resolution. Lastly, I outline potential research directions for evaluating image description systems and other natural language generation applications. Tantalum oxide compounds, with the formula Ta$_2$O$_5$, are distinguished by unique properties including high dielectric values and minimal reflectivity. Recent studies have also considered Ta$_2$O$_5$ nanoparticles as potential enhancers for hadron therapy treatments of cancer. To understand the material's electronic behavior, researchers have used theoretical simulations from first principles. Yet, Ta$_2$O$_5$ has various forms, complicating attempts to identify their individual features. To resolve this issue, researchers used time-dependent density functional methods to study the energy loss function in Ta$_2$O$_5$, specifically in its optical state, and across different polymorphs. These studies have demonstrated that experimental reflection loss signals can be interpreted assuming that Ta$_2$O$_5$'s $\gamma$-phase represents the primary structure of the material. Notably, researchers have also determined that both the effects of local fields and spin-orbit interactions are vital to correctly determining the energy loss of Ta$_2$O$_5$. Lastly, further validating the $\gamma$-Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure, researchers have used a Monte Carlo method to compare calculated reflection loss spectra with the actual results of experiments, achieving a very accurate match. Ultimately, this research has clarified the ground state crystal structure of Ta$_2$O$_5$, establishing it as the $\gamma$-phase, and underscored the significance of both local fields and spin-orbit interactions in determining its energy loss characteristics. Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did not spread primarily through the features of the Reddit platform, but rather was linked to user population size in each state, following a supply-and-demand model. Furthermore, variations in misinformation dissemination were explained by local personality traits and cultural characteristics rather than economic, social, or political conditions. In areas where residents are less diligent in nature, and cultures place little emphasis on adherence to norms, we found increased circulation of all news, including credible sources. Ultimately, our research revealed that The Big Sort's contribution to the dissemination of misinformation was comparable to that of key Reddit platform features and more significant than other local variables. We also explored the timing and content of misinformation dissemination findings. The underlying mechanisms of the supply-and-demand dynamics of misinformation remain unclear and require further investigation. The study's methods and data are available for public scrutiny. The study provides insights into a previously untested hypothesis and offers a unique analytical approach using Reddit data. The findings have implications for the understanding of local influences on the spread of misinformation and the effectiveness of targeted interventions in specific geographical areas. The study also highlights the complexities of information diffusion on social media and the limitations of generalizing findings to other platforms. The research provides a foundation for further exploration of the interplay between geographical and social aspects in the dissemination of misinformation online. The study's data and analytical approaches are available for replication and new analyses. The study identifies avenues for future research, including the examination of new factors, the analysis of different types of misinformation, and the investigation of information diffusion in other geographical contexts. Humans employ spoken language to efficiently teach other people various skills. Although robotic demonstrations are a natural teaching method, learning from solely observed actions does not take full advantage of concurrently heard instructions, which provide additional information. To create more effective robotic learning systems, it's crucial to understand how speech influences demonstrations and if certain speech patterns exist that facilitate robotic learning. This study investigates how humans instruct others through speech while demonstrating manipulative tasks to robots. The research reveals that instructors use a particular pattern of speech, beginning at the start of the task and continuing until the end, which can be broken down into three segments. It also finds that speech is used to draw attention to specific objects, that negation occurs in speech, and that certain instructors repeat the name of objects despite it being clearly visible. The research further explores correlations between speech patterns and various factors including gender, age, and prior robotic teaching experience but finds no significant relationships. To facilitate further development of robotic learning systems, this study also creates a publicly accessible dataset of instruction transcripts and corresponding 3D object manipulation videos. The findings have important implications for the design of future learning systems that combine human instruction with robotic demonstrations. The research provides a foundation for exploring more complex speech patterns and instructions that can greatly enhance the effectiveness of learning systems combining observed and heard information. The newly created dataset, in addition to the study's results, contributes valuable knowledge to the field of robotics that can be used by other researchers. Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these interfaces are being widely used in various settings by many individuals. Although they have achieved considerable success, the infrastructure for automated testing of these systems lags behind traditional software systems. To enhance the quality of conversational systems, developers require a robust automated testing framework that streamlines the process of crafting, executing, and updating test cases. This paper outlines our ongoing research in developing an automated testing framework for conversational agents in Python, and highlights the key challenges faced in this endeavor. Specifically, we highlight the difficulties in establishing a precise specification for desired system behavior and comparing the meaning of utterances. To address these challenges, we rely on a weak formal representation of desired system behavior. Moreover, we introduce a novel approach, called the Inference-based Semantic Comparison, to compare the meaning of utterances. This approach leverages the output of inference modules, which are readily available for open-domain dialogue systems. We also present our framework's functionality from a user's perspective, detailing how to craft, execute, and evaluate tests. Furthermore, we outline our framework's internals, detailing the key components that enable the testing of conversational systems. This includes the weak formal representation of desired system behavior, the inference-based semantic comparison approach, and the testing cycle. Finally, we conclude by outlining potential improvements to our framework, as well as its broader implications for the development of evaluative tools for conversational systems. This paper is accompanied by an executable code repository that demonstrates the applicability of our framework to a real-world dataset. This code repository is available at https://github.com/AmrElsamny/ConverseTest. This work was presented at the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence in 2023. This paper is structured as follows. Section 2 outlines the background and related work in conversational system testing. Section 3 outlines the challenges and the proposed solution in developing an automated testing framework for conversational agents. Section 4 details the design of our framework, Section 5 outlines our experimental evaluation, and Section 6 discusses potential improvements to our framework. This paper concludes in Section 7. This is not a regular paper, but rather an extended abstract for the paper titled "An Automated Testing Framework for Conversational Agents". Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general, domain-agnostic aspect preference. By integrating the domain-specific aspect preference and the domain-agnostic aspect preference, MSDCR attains a thorough understanding of user preferences across each data-poor domain. The empirical evaluations on real-world datasets unequivocally demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models. The proposed approach also yields a lower sparsity threshold than existing single-domain and CDR models, further underscoring its practical utility in addressing pervasive sparsity in real-world scenarios. The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality control to ensure reliable and efficient analysis, especially for extensive research projects. Several approaches have been explored to develop scalable and dependable quality control pipelines, but effectively generalizing these methods across diverse, previously unseen data remains a significant challenge. This study evaluated the MRIQC pipeline, a widely accepted reference, and expanded its assessment to incorporate multiple factors, including but not limited to, scan sites, sequence types, and individual subjects. We analyzed the pipeline's performance using MRI data collected from various sources, including public repositories, through a systematic and methodological approach. The study revealed that while the MRIQC pipeline excels at individual-level quality assessment, it struggles with predictive accuracy when confronted with new, previously unrepresented data, specifically in regards to scan sites, sequences, and certain abnormality categories. Furthermore, we discovered that incorporating additional context, such as subject demographics and imaging parameters, only marginally improves the pipeline's performance. Despite these limitations, the MRIQC pipeline demonstrated robust performance in distinguishing between different quality assessment categories. The study provides a comprehensive framework for evaluating and generalizing MRIQC, as well as similar pipelines, and offers insights into the inherent challenges and necessary precautions when applying such methods in actual research settings. The analysis is further extended to an online platform that enables users to explore the MRIQC pipeline's performance in detail. The underlying data sources and methodology used in this study are also made available to the scientific community through public repositories. The study's findings have important implications for selecting appropriate training data, as well as the necessary caution that should be exercised when interpreting the results obtained from generalizable quality control analyses. This paper examines the structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of GdSn3, CmSn3, and the series GdxCm1-xSn3 ($x = 0.25$, $0.5$, and $0.75$) using a full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method within the generalized gradient approximation+U. We studied the fundamental properties of bulk GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn3 materials crystallizing in the AuCu3 structure. Our results match previous experimental and theoretical data on the GdSn3 compound and indicate that CmSn3 and GdSn3 both adopt a type-A anti-ferromagnetic configuration and display metallic behavior. Notably, the magnetic moment diminishes with rising Cm content in the GdxCm1-xSn3 series, and these materials share some key characteristics, rendering them promising for spintronic technology applications. Additionally, we explored the effects of lattice parameters on the electronic and magnetic properties of the materials and identified the stable range of $c/a$ ratios for these compounds. Furthermore, we provided $c/a$ ratio vs. $x$ graphs for the general GdxCm1-xSn3 series and found that the $c/a$ ratio of CmSn3 lies outside the stable range, which may contribute to its reported instability and explain the difficulty in synthesizing this compound. Lastly, we suggested some possible ways to stabilize CmSn3 and recommended future experimental studies on this compound. Finally, we proposed that the AuCu3 structure of the GdxCm1-xSn3 series could be investigated through experimental means using ab initio calculated X-ray diffraction patterns.

A correlation between this approach and the residual Hubble diagram values of Type Ia supernovae holds a $3.6\sigma$ significance and is consistent with dark matter effects due to galactic halos. As a result, the lens-induced apparent magnitude dispersion will approach the same magnitude as intrinsic SN Ia scatter at $z \approx 1.2$. The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. By developing a method to measure spin-dependent optical transitions, we found that high T center densities located near the interface can exhibit ~1 GHz levels of spectral diffusion without the need for extensive optimization of the fabrication process. Furthermore, we discovered that high T center densities situated further away from the interface, at a depth of 100-110 nm, display ~10 MHz spin-dependent optical transition frequencies, along with significantly longer electron spin relaxation times of up to 1.3 ms and nuclear spin memory durations of up to 10 ms. These findings indicate that SOI technology offers a promising path towards efficient and controlled quantum lightmatter interactions within the O-band region. This paper undertakes a mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely used, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. Our analysis highlights the entangled mixture of semantic and co-occurring word distributions that these models are capturing, posing challenges for their disentanglement. Our work offers a mathematical framework for the word2vec model, uncovering its underlying assumptions and the structured hypotheses it implicitly tests about the data. We also explore the ability of these models to extend to sequential learning tasks, suggesting that they can learn from the temporal dependencies in our financial corpus. Our research has implications for the widespread application of these models in fields like natural language processing, finance, and economics. We emphasize the importance of interpreting embeddings in the context of the data generating process and caution against overinterpreting the semantic meanings of these embeddings without considering the distribution of the co-occurring terms. We also outline potential avenues for disentangling the semantic from the frequentist components of these embeddings, suggesting that current word2vec implementations are, in effect, learning the Markov chain of a corpus rather than the intrinsic meanings of words. Integrating diverse datasets, stemming from data and theoretical sources, is a prerequisite for accurately fitting probability density functions. While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. Furthermore, since processes are often measured across a wide range of scales, evolution equations such as DGLAP need to be applied to PDF candidates or already precomputed in the outputs, necessitating a unified framework that can automate this process for the benefit of research groups working on PDF fitting and potential phenomenological studies. To address this challenge, we present a theoretical pipeline that combines the predictions of different processes affected by PDFs, with the capability to treat outputs from various PDF fit methods. This pipeline is composed of processes like deep learning based PDF fitting and traditional methods using standard codes, with interfaces allowing users to modify the process combinations and PDF fit frameworks. To facilitate seamless integration, we provide detailed documentation on the pipeline's structure and components. The theoretical pipeline is capable of automate tasks, offering user-friendly options for configuring processes and PDF combinations, as well as providing graphical representations of underlying physics through plots of process outputs with respect to energy scales and different PDF fit combinations. With the ability to manage up to thousand of intermediate output files, this pipeline is suitable for various research settings, from individual users to large-scale collaborative groups. The code for this pipeline is available at https://github.com/AlaminHossain/Theory-Pipeline-for-PDF-Fitting.

We introduce MG-GLAM, a computational tool developed to rapidly create comprehensive N-body simulations for various cosmological theories, specifically modified gravity models. This program builds upon the existing GLAM code and incorporates an advanced multigrid method to solve the non-linear equations characteristic of modified gravity theories, resulting in highly efficient simulations. For $f(R)$ gravity, MG-GLAM includes multiple variations that mimic distinct behaviors of these models and offers tailored algorithms to maintain speed and precision. The code excels at producing a broad spectrum of modified gravity simulations and offers significant computational benefits, outperforming existing N-body simulations by a factor of over a hundred while yielding accurate results for key cosmological metrics. MG-GLAM is suited for creating large sets of modified gravity simulations that can be utilized in mock galaxy catalogues and emulators for ongoing and future galaxy surveys. Ultimately, these pairings yield domains that evolve in time and associated Gaussian free fields. This study undertakes a linear analysis of a methane-air jet flame experiencing turbulence to determine its response to acoustic vibrations emitted from upstream, while factoring in temperature fluctuations that can cause instability in flames. Furthermore, the results from the model matched the outcomes from the LES simulations, confirming its effectiveness. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses exhibit recurring X-ray bursts within short intervals. Improving neural conversational agents' ability to produce diverse, engaging responses in casual conversations is a challenge. To tackle this issue, this paper introduces two significant innovations. Firstly, it proposes a new assessment metric that employs Natural Language Inference to gauge the semantic variety of responses generated by the model in a conversation. Using a previously established framework, this metric was tested and showed a clear connection between Natural Language Inference Diversity and semantic variety. It was discovered that the contradiction relation yields more precise results than the neutral relation in measuring diversity and integrating the Natural Language Inference Threshold to remove trivial entailments yields a 6% improvement in the correlation with human assessors. Secondly, this paper demonstrates a way to enhance the semantic variety of responses generated by the model through a simple yet effective technique that incorporates Natural Language Inference as an auxiliary objective. When evaluated using the newly proposed metric, this technique resulted in a 5% improvement in Natural Language Inference Diversity. It was discovered that NLI Diversity is comprised of three elements: (1) a initial base value that remains steady throughout conversations, (2) a value directly tied to the number of response options, and (3) a value tied to the conversation topic. Furthermore, this paper presents a simple yet effective technique to control NLI Diversity and examined various ways to do so, finding that the number of response options, the NLU relation, the threshold, and the conversation topic all significantly impact NLI Diversity. Finally, this paper demonstrated the practical utility of the proposed NLI Diversity metric by conducting a user study in which human assessors preferred the model that generated responses with higher NLI Diversity. The code for this project is available at github.com/pudoi/nni-ddiv.

The occurrence of sustainable hydrogen burning in very low-mass stars might be impacted by rotation due to the addition of centrifugal force and potential break-up caused by rapid spinning. Computer simulations model rotating low-mass stars with the capability for sustained nuclear reactions, considering a range of rotation rates, rather than slow rotation alone. Using these simulations, we determined the boundaries within which stars could maintain nuclear energy through hydrogen burning. These boundaries varied based on angular momentum. However, above a certain threshold (approximately 8.85 x 10^48 erg s) the boundaries broke into two distinct branches, resulting from objects losing mass and experiencing extreme spin. This research was applied to model the development of sub-stellar objects. Two possible scenarios were modeled: one with external forces gradually slowing the star, mainly controlled by spin-down time, and another where the star spins out of control, ultimately shedding mass and shrinking. In the second case, the simulation reached its limiting point, but not quite reaching the point of disintegration. This research also provides equations that define these limiting points, which could be important for the study of sub-stellar objects formed through gravitational collapse. Additionally, this study demonstrates that computer simulations can recover known results, but with more realistic conditions, and also recovers similar results from earlier studies, but with a more comprehensive understanding. Furthermore, this research on the computer simulations suggests that the added rotation causes stars to shed mass at higher masses, but also added rotation causes the star to shed mass at lower masses due to extreme spin, which was not previously considered. This could have implications for the occurrence of sustainable energy through hydrogen burning in very low-mass stars and their rotation. This research on the computer simulations also model the development of sub-stellar objects up to their point of disintegration, which could have implications for their remaining structure after disintegration. Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free (planar) drawing. The question of determining if an edge-free representation exists after breaking at most a specified number of nodes remains tractable in relation to that number. The article presents an iterative procedure for achieving this condition, with performance analysis indicating its efficiency meets the criteria of a problem tackled in polynomial time with respect to the number of nodes split. In addition to its applicability to bipartite graphs, the method can also be applied to general graph drawings, with the process being inspectable and potentially useful for related problems. The article further includes a discussion on the relationship between node splitting and other problems, as well as the presence of a straightforward connection to the parameterized problem of detecting cliques. The proposed algorithm can be employed as a component within larger frameworks, such as tools for interactive visualization tools, with the article offering implementation details to facilitate integration with existing software platforms. The research underlying this article has been conducted as part of the authors' involvement with the Science Experience program aimed at engaging high school students in collaborative scientific projects. Becker-Denef-Lipschitz first observed in 1979 that over finite fields $k$, the total residue map $\text{res}$ from Laurent series to $k$ is expressible in a specific language, provided $t$ is included as a parameter. This discovery motivated further research into the properties of a specific mathematical theory related to valued fields. In the course of these investigations, the authors proved that this theory does not have a certain desirable feature and demonstrated that, for infinite fields $k$, the associated power series fields cannot be computationally decided. This, in turn, led to an analogous undecidability conclusion for a specific complex-valued field of power series. This paper aims to present a more accessible path to these undecidability results by introducing a simpler decision procedure for fields based on non-archimedean norms over the real numbers and highlighting the implications of this approach for the associated power series fields. This decision procedure can be used to show that the theory associated with the field of rational functions in a single indeterminate over the real numbers is computationally decidable when equipped with a specific non-archimedean norm. This, in turn, enables a more elementary proof of the undecidability of the field based on power series over the real numbers. This paper also explores some related research questions and offers a suitable generalization of the Becker-Denef-Lipschitz observation. This generalization can be applied to demonstrate that the field based on power series over the complex numbers is also computationally undecidable. This paper's findings represent an enhancement over the original Becker-Denef-Lipschitz result and provide a novel undecidability proof for the field based on power series over the complex numbers. This approach differs from the original research presented in [1] and offers an originally unresearched question an affirmative answer. In order to enhance side-channel attacks, this research introduces a new technique, HyperDegrade, which incorporates previous methods and employs simultaneous multithreading architectures.  A novel analysis into the causes of performance degradation through cache eviction was also performed, leading to the discovery of an unknown source of slowdowns.  Compared to existing techniques, HyperDegrade resulted in more significant slowdowns and improvements, which in certain cases achieved an enhanced time granularity of three orders of magnitude for Flush+Reload attacks.  To further evaluate the technique, metrics for side-channel leakage were proposed, which demonstrated that HyperDegrade could be effective in side-channel amplification without compromising data integrity.  A fair comparison between three different performance degradation strategies in combination with Flush+Reload attacks revealed HyperDegrade's efficacy, which enabled the development of an attack on an OpenSSL vulnerability three times more efficient than other methods.  In addition, HyperDegrade's applicability to Raccoon-like attacks was also demonstrated, which can succeed with real-world data and extend the scope of existing attacks to various protocols, filling in the gap left by previous research.  Full implementation details, experimental evidence, and theoretical analysis of HyperDegrade are provided, which showcase the technique's versatility and efficiency in enhancing side-channel attacks, making it suitable for various purposes including research, prototyping, and real-world exploitation.  A specialized tool for HyperDegrade is available at https://github.com/0xPortia/HyperDegrade.  A note on ethics and detection of side-channel attacks is also included, which discusses the challenges faced in developing effective countermeasures against such attacks and highlights the difficulties in detecting side-channel leakage due to its dependence on hardware and the diverse range of available CPUs.  In conclusion, this research demonstrates the practical applications of HyperDegrade in enhancing side-channel attacks, which can be adapted to work with various protocols and provide valuable insights into performance degradation, which can be employed in the development of future attacks. A distinguished property of unknoting operations is that they can be used to demonstrate the equivalence of two link embeddings. Unknoting operations can be further classified into either local unknoting operations, which rely on the presence of a specific link component, or global unknoting operations, which can untangle an embedded circle regardless of its source. It is proven that unknoting operations can be used to determine the equivalence of two long knot projections. Furthermore, methods are provided for constructing unknoting operations from a long knot, and it is demonstrated that the number of unknoting operations generated in this manner is directly related to the number of long knot projections that can be created from the same knot. Additionally, unknoting operations are found to be sensitive to the specific long knot projection used, as they are able to distinguish between long knot projections. Utilizing unknoting operations, it is possible to establish the existence of an infinite number of distinct long knot projections. In cooperative systems with multiple agents, coordination enables tasks to be performed that would be beyond the capabilities of any single agent. We investigate the concept of coordination through strategic decision-making, focusing on a scenario where agents make informed decisions about whether to coordinate with others and with which partners. This decision is crucial, as it directly affects the efficiency of the system and is susceptible to abuse through malicious behavior. We develop a mathematical framework to study this phenomenon using a cooperative game theory framework known as a stochastic hot-potato game. This framework allows us to examine how cooperation emerges in a system consisting of multiple agents connected through a network. We identify specific conditions under which cooperative behavior can be sustained and establish that, in general, cooperation is fragile and easily disrupted. These findings are illustrated through numerical examples and simplified analytical models. This research also explores the potential benefits of mobile agents and the impact of a physical environment on the efficiency of a system. We discuss the connection to other games and various possible generalizations of this model. Furthermore, we provide an appendix detailing a specific algorithm for computing cooperative equilibria. This research contributes to the broader field of cooperative systems, particularly in relation to autonomous vehicles, microgrids, and robotic systems. The underlying challenges are relevant to a wide range of complex systems and have implications for how cooperation and stability can be encouraged through appropriate design and management. The corresponding code for this research is available at https://github.com/AayushKrishna/ShpG. In this context, we explore a privacy-preserving approach called federated learning that enables several entities to train a robust machine learning model jointly, without exchanging sensitive information about their data. Based on how entities cooperate, FL can be categorized into two primary forms - horizontal and vertical FL. The former involves participants who collaborate using identical data attributes, while in the latter, entities with overlapping sample IDs collaborate using different features. Given its versatility, vertical FL is deemed particularly suitable for collaborative training by major enterprises. Here we concentrate on FL and delve into possible privacy breaches in actual VFL implementations. Two applicable attacks were created by us - one is called a reverse multiplication attack designed to compromise privacy when the ratio of categories to features is small, and the other, a reverse sum attack, effective even when that ratio is substantial. The effectiveness of these attacks was validated through actual deployments and simulations. Moreover, available literature highlights the operational costs and necessary data category ratios for both attacks. Lastly, precautions were outlined to mitigate these privacy-breaching incidents. Our research highlights the challenges and potential security threats of actual VFL implementations, presenting transferable attack methods that can also be applicable to horizontal FL. Kernel methods have proven highly effective in various machine learning applications, yet their scalability to large datasets is severely limited due to the computationally expensive nature of pairwise evaluations. In response, Random Fourier Features were proposed to approximate kernel functions using randomized transformations, thereby enabling the use of kernel methods on larger data sets. While widely adopted, this method has significant drawbacks, notably requiring fixed and non-adaptive transformation dimensions, which are determined independently of the data in question. As a result, this method often falls short of providing a true linear reduction in dimensionality, with multiple studies demonstrating its equivalence to a linear projection based on the input data, resulting projections which, in turn, can be just as computationally expensive as the original kernel method. In an attempt to address these limitations, this study introduces an alternative method grounded in the same Random Fourier Features framework but with a range of data-dependent dimensions, which can be accurately estimated using a combination of the original feature map dimensions and the pairwise inner product of the data at hand. Furthermore, this study provides theoretical guarantee on the proposed method's accuracy as well as an analytical expression for its expected computational overhead, which is found to be equivalent to $O(nk^2+d^2)$ in contrast to the $O(nd^2)$ overhead of the standard method. To support and validate this analysis, this study accompanies a comprehensive set of numerical experiments covering a broad range of applications, from linear classification to nonlinear regression, with both synthetic and real-world data sets. As expected, the proposed method outperforms the standard Random Fourier Features method across all scenarios examined. In addition to its individual value, this study also incorporates a previously published technique, with which it demonstrates the feasibility of combining methods to enhance the basic Random Fourier Features framework. As such, this study provides an extensive set of algorithms, for which it makes available the underlying code. With its strengths in both linear and nonlinear approximations, this study proposes a method that can be used by itself or in conjunction with other methods to solve a range of machine learning problems. In our study, we demonstrated how both a group that operates on a set in a recurring manner and a diagonal group are effectively incorporated into the wreath products under their combined, or product action, utilizing the Cartesian Decomposition technique. We then provide specific examples of how this method can be applied to a variety of groups, including abelian groups, cyclic groups, direct products of groups, and more complex structures like the symmetric group S_n operating on the index set {1,...,n}. Furthermore, we derive an explicit formula for calculating the dimension of the wreath product. Alongside this, we establish a connection between the Frobenius-Prikry formula and the Cartesian Decomposition method. Additionally, we explore the applicability of this approach to both regular and irregular group actions. Lastly, we demonstrate how this method can be utilized to determine the structure of the monoid formed by the wreath products of a group operating on a set in a recurring manner. This research was conducted in collaboration with T. Timar.

Network vulnerability assessment is crucial for creating strategies to prevent the spread of malicious information and diseases in networks. Researchers often study network immunization, but traditional approaches typically focus on broad measures, such as network criticality and component size. In contrast, this paper delves into a micro-level analysis, where the removal of individual nodes during an attack is examined in detail. Specifically, this paper investigates the number of nodes that become disconnected from the main component as a result of removing one node. A key factor for maintaining stability in future low-carbon power grids is expected to be energy storage systems. Studies examining past experiences reveal a common issue with storage units - they frequently fail to take advantage of high-price signals during periods of low energy supply. This behavior has been often attributed to inaccurate forecasting or operational issues. However, our research suggests a more plausible explanation is rooted in risk-averse decision-making practices. Utilizing a stochastic self-scheduling approach and real data from the Australian electricity market, our findings show that risk-conscious storage units prioritize short-term cost savings by engaging in local price speculation, and tend to ignore opportunities in periods with unusual price fluctuations. This has significant policy implications, given the difficulty of detecting and managing storage units' risk aversion. Moreover, it highlights the importance of addressing this issue through appropriate regulatory and market design frameworks. This work also contributes to the development of risk-aware storage unit models, with implications for grid management and power trading. Lastly, our findings have broader applications to other behind-the-meter assets that can respond to local signals.

Simply enhancing a machine learning model's accuracy is not sufficient, as we must also focus on increasing its reliability. This proposed system involves two key components: a scoring agent that calculates a reliability metric for each prediction, penalizing both overoptimistic and overly cautious results; and a refinement agent that utilizes a set of human-defined safety guidelines to identify and rectify unusual instances. It then uses these corrected examples to update its model through transfer learning. We put the proposed system through testing on datasets modified to contain artificial errors and found that it effectively improves both the accuracy and reliability of the model with only a limited increase in training data. Furthermore, the system's efficiency enables it to be applied to real-time scenarios. The proposed approach has the advantage of being straightforward and can be combined with existing models without significant difficulty. We also explore the potential expansion of the system to incorporate other methods of model refinement. A newly defined polynomial, referred to as the nth toroidal colored Jones polynomial, is established for links in a thickened torus. Dubbed $J_n^T$, this polynomial demonstrates numerous properties similar to the original colored Jones polynomial, and notably displays volume conjecture behavior. By applying $J_n^T$, we prove the volume conjecture holds true for a specific link, and provide computational data suggesting it holds for additional links. Moreover, $J_n^T$ can be represented through two distinct constructions, a pseudo-operator invariant, and a construction rooted in the Kauffman bracket skein module of the torus. Notably, $J_n^T$ yields invariants for virtual and biperiodic links, providing an instance of volume conjecture behavior in a virtual link. The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC detected the production of top quarks for the first time using proton-lead data at an 8.16 TeV nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy. Top quark production was identified in events featuring one isolated electron or muon and four or more jets, from a data set totaling 174 inverse nanobarns of luminosity. The measured signal exceeded the five-standard-deviation threshold expected for a background-only hypothesis, and the cross-sectional measurement for top quark pairs was found to be 45 nanobarns with an 8-nanobarn uncertainty, consistent with theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics. This finding also marked the first for quark production in proton-nucleus collisions. Correcting for the lack of longitudinal polarisation in proton-lead data, the measured cross-section deviated from the predicted value by 1.9 standard deviations with an additional 0.5-standard-deviation uncertainty. This study utilized approximately 0.6 nanobarns of proton-proton data at a 8.16 TeV center-of-mass energy for calibration and background suppression, with the remaining 174 nanobarns available through the upgrade to the CMS detector for the upcoming LHC run. The measured cross-section was also expressed in terms of forward charged particle multiplicity, with results indicating that the average multiplicity per nucleon must exceed 2.4 in order to produce top quarks. This finding was comparable to estimates from Monte Carlo simulations with the AMPT and PYTHIA generators. The study demonstrated the capability of the CMS detector for measuring processes involving large systems of hadrons and identified key physics for the LHC run with lead-lead collisions at a 5.02 TeV nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy. The measured cross-section for top quark production in proton-nucleus collisions has important implications for studies involving heavy quark production in nuclear medium and was used to guide the interpretation of corresponding measurements in lead-lead collisions. The observed process demonstrated the necessity for next-to-next-to-leading order quantum chromodynamics calculations in proton-nucleus and nucleon-nucleon collisions at high energies. We investigated the absorption of a single, monochromatic light beam at 689 nm as it passes through a cloud of ultracold $^{88}$Sr atoms. Due to the interaction, the absorption pattern deviates significantly, taking on an asymmetric shape as a result of a shift in frequency that is equivalent in magnitude to the natural width of a specific atomic transition in strontium. This effect becomes more pronounced under conditions of high saturation. Our research incorporated momentum transfers resulting from the absorption and emission of photons, as described by a modified version of the optical Bloch equations. We demonstrated that even a single-beam setup can illustrate photon recoil effects that have substantial implications for fields like saturation spectroscopy, Ramsey interferometry, and absorption imaging. In particular, we found that a shift of the central frequency by one natural line width can occur when using a light source with high coherence when the light and the atoms are moving at similar speeds. In such cases, it's essential to ensure that the light frequency is matched to the atomic frequency with high precision, a requirement that also applies to other phenomena like light shift or Stark effect, that can also cause a frequency shift in the absorption pattern. We also explored the relationship between this effect and other relevant parameters, incorporating the width of the light source, the velocity of the atoms and the light, as well as the power of the light beam. As a result, we derived a general formula that can be used to determine the frequency shift in a wide range of scenarios, from low to high saturation, and with or without the light source's contribution to the velocity of the atoms and the light. Notably, this approach can be applied to other atomic species by simply interchanging the natural frequency of strontium with that of the target species. In addition to this main finding, our research also highlighted the importance of properly accounting for the contribution of velocity-dependent light shift, which can result from the interaction between the light and the atoms, with the latter moving at high speeds. This can be achieved by either modulating the velocity of the atoms, modulating the velocity of the light, or a combination of both, with the aim of obtaining precise information about the atomic energy levels, with the help of velocity-dependent light shift, Doppler broadening, and absorption spectra. All of these effects can be incorporated into a single, unified equation that can be applied to a wide range of scenarios, from low to high saturation, and with or without the light source's contribution to the velocity of the atoms and the light,

When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of dense mixtures undergo a sudden and extreme thickening, characterized by a transition from fluid-like behavior to rigidity. Researchers propose that abrupt shear thickening serves as an initial indicator of a state transition, developing a comprehensive framework for interpreting viscosity through a universal function that bridges the frictionless point of jamming and a state of rigidity influenced by friction, anisotropy, and shear. Studies involving cornstarch in glycerol and silica spheres in glycerol found that for these two systems, viscosity can be condensed into a singular, stress- and volume fraction-independent curve, revealing distinct scaling regimes that reflect different universality classes and implying that isotropic and anisotropic shear jamming have unique characteristics. Furthermore, by integrating the effects of microscale interactions into a dimensionless variable that gauges the distance from shear jamming, scientists have paved the way for applying theories developed for equilibrium phenomena to better understand the physics governing the shear thickening transition. The universality of these results is expected to hold true for all dense mixtures, cementing the status of the shear thickening transition as a fundamental, universal phenomenon. The research presented here is featured in the paper published in the journal Nature Physics volume 19, page 1341-1346 (2023). The associated code is publicly available at GitHub repository https://github.com/ShearThickeningGroup. The researchers encourage other scientists to build upon their work and integrate new data into the analytical framework for the sake of advancing our understanding of the physics governing the shear thickening transition. The code used for the figures and calculations can be found in the supplementary information. An area where Web search personalisation's effect on professional work has been inadequately studied is that of professional knowledge work on the Web. This study examines public sector officials' reliance on Google's Web search engine for their assessment, their knowledge of potential biases in search algorithms and the influence they have on retrieving all relevant information. The study's results show that a substantial number of the participants are unaware of potential biases in search algorithms and the possible strategies to prevent them from overlooking essential information. Notably, our data reveal that as much as 20% of the necessary information may go undetected due to the influence of Web search personalisation. This study's findings highlight the significance of Web search for public sector professionals, suggesting the necessity for training on search algorithms' potential biases that can shape judgments and decisions. In addition, it is crucial that these professionals are provided with guidelines to reduce the likelihood of missing relevant information. This study's results also contribute to Web search personalisation research by offering insights into the effect of search engine bias on users' ability to find all the information they need. This information on search engine bias can be useful to develop strategies for reducing it. Not to be overlooked is the broader implication of this research for individuals using search engines in similar professional knowledge work settings. This study used a survey method to gather data from a sample of 309 public sector officials in Sri Lanka. It used a structured questionnaire to collect primary data on Web search practices, officials' knowledge of search algorithms' potential biases and the influence these biases have on retrieving all relevant information. The data were analysed using descriptive and inferential statistical methods. This study suggests several recommendations, including training public sector officials on search algorithms' potential biases that can shape judgments and decisions, providing them with guidelines to reduce the likelihood of missing relevant information, conducting further research into Web search practices and the effect of search engine bias on users' ability to find all the information they need. In addition, it proposes developing strategies for reducing search engine bias that can shape judgments and decisions. A novel approach is proposed to create and assess a respiratory motion-compensated four-dimensional T2-weighted MRI sequence, which is crucial in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. Data acquisition is continuous via a spiral acquisition method with reordering of Cartesian sampling points (rCASPR) that ensures matching image contrast and sorts data into respiratory phases. Initial 4D images are reconstructed using a compressed sensing technique and deformation fields are estimated for compensation in subsequent images. Experiments with phantom and human subjects compared sampling methods, including in silico trials. Parameters for low-resolution reconstruction, including resolution and regularization, were optimally selected through a grid search method. Motion compensation in rCASPR was tested in eight subjects with results indicating better point-spread-function in rCASPR with little difference in contrast, thus making it feasible for direct application in radiology and radiotherapy treatments. Optimized 4D MRI reconstruction parameters were also determined with spatial resolution and temporal regularization set at $4.5mm^3$ and $10^{-4}$. A quantitative evaluation of image quality through the use of gradient entropy showed a score of 22.02 for motion-compensated rCASPR. Ultimately, this rCASPR-based method provides high-quality, free-breathing MRI images that minimize alterations in scan duration and image contrast, allowing direct application in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. This has implications for radiotherapy treatments of organs subject to significant respiratory movement, such as lungs, liver, and parts of the abdomen, with scan durations that range from 12 seconds to 12 minutes for low-to-high respiratory motion speeds. The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has long relied on testing the statistical significance of differences in performance. This test aims to verify that observed discrepancies aren't simply coincidental. Despite the importance of accurate results, a lack of suitable exact algorithms forces practitioners to use time-consuming Monte Carlo approximations to achieve this goal. In contrast, we've developed an efficient method for calculating paired-permutation test results exactly. This exact algorithm takes significantly less time to compute than Monte Carlo methods. In particular, we observed a 10 times speedup when using our exact algorithm versus the commonly employed Monte Carlo approximation on a representative dataset of 20000 samples. Furthermore, our method enables the use of more stringent significance levels that Monte Carlo methods cannot achieve with similar computation times. This exact algorithm can be incorporated into various NLP systems, including NLP platform NLPX, NLP library PyKT, and search-based supervised learning methods. Our results also demonstrate that this exact algorithm can be executed on a standard laptop. In addition to this, we explored the feasibility of using this exact algorithm on larger datasets and discovered that while it can be done, it requires the use of more powerful computing resources. This is particularly true for datasets containing over 100000 samples. Alongside this, we examined the different data structures that can be employed to implement this exact algorithm and identified the most suitable ones. In particular, we found that using a pre-sorting data structure results in the most desirable performance. Alongside this, we discovered that the frequently advised random permutation method is not suitable for this purpose. In fact, it is no better than simply using a plain list. In conclusion, our research focused on the efficient calculation of paired-permutation test results. This is critical for various NLP tasks that rely heavily on testing the statistical significance of differences in performance. We define loom spaces as a more general framework incorporating leaf spaces for pseudo-Anosov flows and link spaces for veering triangulations. Building on Gu\'eritaud's research, it is demonstrated that there is a veering triangulation inherently linked to every loom space, with this triangulation's realization being topologically equivalent to 3D space. Additionally, this triangulation's combinatorial properties are explicitly determined by the loom's combinatorial data. Furthermore, the boundaries of loom spaces are topologically equivalent to the 2D surface of a veering triangulation, with this surface's realization being derived from the realization of the associated veering triangulation. The relationship between loom and veering triangulation spaces also provides a new insight: the triangulation's vertices are topologically equivalent to the 0-dimensional boundary of the loom space. The process of transitioning from loom to veering triangulation spaces is achieved through a sequence of specialized branch cuts, with these cuts enabling the recovery of the veering triangulation's combinatorial data from the loom space. The proposed framework is then applied to investigate the properties of veering triangulations through the loom space lens, focusing on the surface's boundaries and branch cuts.
