This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. By employing this strategy, BNPS yields an optimized model performance and a notable decrease in false positives. To further address the challenging low-frequency proposals with spatial ambiguity, we refine the spatial modeling capability of SABRA in two ways: introducing a simple and efficient multi-head graph attention network to capture global object interactions and a spatial mask decoder that learns the local configuration. Our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art methods across three datasets for human-object interaction and visual relationship detection. Moreover, our findings are supported by comprehensive analysis and experimental evaluations. The code for this project is available online at https://github.com/zwang-cse/SABRA.

We've performed an in-depth analysis of three galaxy cores at $\rm z=2.91$ within a massive galaxy group, yielding high-resolution infrared and submillimeter data. This revealed that the galaxies exhibit extremely compact, actively star-forming cores at the centers of massive, irregularly shaped disk systems, both of which exhibit quiescent, lopsided characteristics. Consequently, these galaxies are witnessing `outside-in' quenching. We propose a theoretical framework suggesting that mass asymmetry, resulting from absorbed and irregular matter, is accountable for their diminished star-formation activity by channeling it towards their core. Furthermore, we observe that disk asymmetry is associated with gas streams that are feeding the galaxies and influencing their evolution. This is manifested by an aligned major-axis of galaxies in relation to nearby filaments, presenting observational evidence of accretion streams on galaxy evolution. This is demonstrated by bulge construction, combined with massive quiescent, lopsided galaxies in the current stage, until they collide with a major merger galaxy. This interaction eventually transforms these galaxies into irregularly shaped, massive elliptical galaxies similar to massive elliptical galaxies at $\rm z \approx 1$.

Recently discovered solar observations from Bolivia (5250 m above sea level) and Mexico (4600 m above sea level) uncovered a significant event on November 7, 2004, linked to a powerful X2.0 solar flare. Analysis of recorded data, along with satellite observations from GOES 11 and SOHO, suggest that neutrons may have broken down into electrons and protons. Historically, evidence of this process was found on board ISEE3 on June 3rd, 1982 and through ground detectors in Goose Bay and Deep River on October 19th, 1989, providing a second terrestrial instance of this occurrence. Calculated neutron flux rates vary depending on detection methods but indicate a rather high rate of 1.3 x 10^9 per steradian. Notably, this event departs from the typical solar neutron event profile observed at high altitudes, offering new insights into solar physics and neutron detection methodologies. Moreover, satellite data failed to capture this level of neutron flux, highlighting the importance of ground-based observations in recording such events. The observed electron/proton ratios in Bolivia and Mexico exceeded previous recorded solar neutron terrestrially induced effects by nearly a factor of six, further underscoring the significance of this event. The recently discovered data also bring to light the capabilities of existing ground-based detectors in Mexico and highlight the potential for similar detectors in other high-altitude locations around the globe. Lastly, the Nov 7, 2004 solar flare/neutron decay proton event or a similar event may have been recorded at other high-altitude observation sites, suggesting the possibility of recovering archived data from various locations to gain a more comprehensive understanding of this phenomenon. The novel analysis and discovery presented here are the result of a collaborative effort involving researchers from Mexico, the United States, and Bolivia. This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. To validate our findings, we updated the constraints based on spectroscopic surface measurements, verified that the detected oscillation patterns align with the previously determined core and outer layer rotation rates, and confirmed that the star exhibits no significant chemical abnormalities. Additionally, we eliminated the possibility of any interaction with a companion star that might be causing tidal forces. Lastly, we examined possible explanations for this unusual internal rotation profile, including the possibility of the star ingesting a giant planet or experiencing enhanced angular momentum redistribution through tidal inertial waves induced by a nearby substellar companion, and encouraged future observational and theoretical studies. As the first detected instance of this internal rotation pattern, KIC 9267654's unique characteristics offer valuable insights into the angular momentum behavior within low-mass giant stars. As such, we propose design elements for future missions that could detect similar phenomena in similar stars. As for the particular case of KIC 9267654, we recommend monitoring the star's light curves and oscillation spectra closely, as well as conducting in-depth investigations into its primordial rotation rate, as well as the characteristics of any companion stars that might be influencing its evolution. Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their effectiveness significantly declines when they are applied to emerging events. This limitation creates a significant obstacle for the current methods in detecting false news on unexpected events. Furthermore, the fact that newly emerging events necessitate building a new model from scratch or retraining the existing one, which is often expensive, time-consuming and impractical in real-world settings. To address this challenge, an end-to-end fake news detection system called MetaFEND has been proposed, allowing for the rapid learning to identify false information on unexpected events with limited information from verified sources. This system leverages the strength of both meta-learning and neural process methods, incorporates a module to address label embedding, and employs a hard attention mechanism to enhance the effectiveness by dealing with category information and eliminating unnecessary information. Experiments conducted on large multimedia datasets obtained from Twitter and Weibo demonstrate the effectiveness of the MetaFEND system in detecting false information on previously unseen events and outperforms the current state-of-the-art techniques. Moreover, the system's capability in handling multiple modalities has been validated through a series of ablation studies. Code for the proposed method is available at: https://github.com/ghaithan/MetaFEND.

Quantum tunneling is an inherent process that lacks a direct analogy in classical physics, and it can rival Coulomb interactions to give rise to intricate phenomena.
In silicon, precise placement of phosphorus dopants is feasible to address the diverse consequences of this interplay, however this approach depends on wave functions related to crystal symmetry, which quantum tunneling inherently affects.
In this study, lattice-aperiodic valley interference patterns were directly visualized in silicon by employing scanning tunneling microscopy to investigate coupled atoms.
The examination reveals the significance of envelope anisotropy, valley interference and the location of the dopants on Heisenberg's spin exchange interaction in silicon.
The findings indicate that exchange interaction becomes immune to valley interference by arranging in-plane dopants in particular directions aligned with the crystallographic orientation, ultimately retrieving vacuum-like characteristics where the exchange interaction maximizes the overlap between donor orbitals, and the variation in pairs is minimized to less than 10-fold.
This robust exchange interaction remains over a considerable distance range, from a high-fidelity quantum computation regime influenced by Coulomb interaction to coupled donor arrays used in quantum simulations in silicon.

Complex systems consisting of multiple interacting components typically adhere to straightforward and universal principles, which underpin their intricate behaviors. Despite graph neural networks offering valuable insights for modeling these complex interactions, there's still a significant gap in understanding how to effectively generalize to novel instances of the same system type. In our investigation, we successfully applied graph neural networks to analyze a representative example of a nonlinear dynamical system – the belief propagation algorithm. By interpreting the learned representations and network components, we revealed their alignment with fundamental properties of the underlying probabilistic inference algorithm. Furthermore, we established a key relationship between the network's statistical interactions and its parameter configuration, which we termed the 'graph translator'. Leveraging this translator enabled us to explore two novel generalization capabilities. Firstly, we could extract the underlying structure of an unexplored system from observational time series data, without needing explicit access to the system itself. Secondly, we could generate a corresponding network from this recovered structure, paving the way for a deeper understanding of the dynamics and underlying architecture of complex systems and demonstrating the practical applications of this insight for future generalization. Our research findings are supported by comprehensive numerical experiments presented in this study. Our novel approach, consisting of the graph translator and its associated translator module, can be used as a foundation for future generalization, following which we discuss three specific scenarios – simple probabilistic inference algorithms, hidden parameter networks, and linear time series systems – to further demonstrate its practical usefulness. Our code is available online at https://github.com/ghul123/grab. Our research findings are also presented at the ICML 2020 workshop on Interpretable Machine Learning. A cutting-edge, minimally invasive therapy called Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) treats seizures caused by epilepsy in a specific brain area, the mesial temporal lobe. Evaluating the effectiveness of this treatment requires analyzing changes to the treated brain area after LITT, which can be achieved by accurately defining the treated region through image processing. Although deep learning techniques offer high precision in defining this region, training them requires a large amount of data which can be hard to obtain for a new and emerging treatment such as LITT. In response, this paper proposes two novel approaches to generate multiple brain images that simulate different stages of the therapy, which can train and evaluate precursors to these deep learning models. These precursors then improve these deep learning models by fine-tuning them with generated data, resulting in better performance compared to traditional evaluation methods when tested on real-world data. Furthermore, the proposed framework can be used to synthesize data for other therapeutic interventions similar to LITT. The code for this project is available online at https://github.com/ghrasoul/BrainLesionSynthesis. GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, leveraging graph transformation rules to ease these tasks. However, efficiently developing GP 2 programs poses difficulties, primarily stemming from the time-consuming nature of graph matching. To overcome this limitation, the GP 2 framework incorporates a type of rooted rule that can be matched rapidly, given certain conditions are met. In order to accelerate the GP 2 compiler, several key modifications have been made to Bak's compiler, including a data structure optimisation for dynamic arrays known as BigArray. This novel structure, characterised by successive size increments of its components, enhances compiler performance. As evidence of the compiler's speed-enhancing benefits, a case study is presented showcasing the GP 2 compiler's application in optimising the runtime efficiency of a program aimed at detecting binary DAGs. This previously time-consuming operation is now executed at a linear rate following the compiler upgrade. Furthermore, the upgraded GP 2 compiler, coupled with a recently developed GP 2 interpreter, enables rapid program execution on top of the GP 2 semantics, facilitated through a loop that iteratively applies rooted rules until a stabilising state is reached. This development opens the door to exploring the GP 2 semantics at high speeds, as demonstrated by a simple simulation involving a complex network. Lastly, the upgraded compiler's efficacy in evaluating the validity of graphs according to a set of defined rules is also illustrated. These enhancements to the GP 2 compiler are available online, ready for use by the research community.

Dimensionality reduction in high-dimensional data is effectively managed using a prominent method called the Feature Extraction network, which has different types such as Encoder and Augmentor. Encoder-based methods encode the data into a compact representation by utilizing an encoder network. They provide superior performance but are prone to overfitting due to the large number of parameters in the encoder. In contrast, Augmentor-based methods reduce the dimensionality by manipulating the input data with transformation networks, which have fewer parameters. However, these methods are often hampered by the selection of pre-defined transformation techniques, resulting in suboptimal performance. This study introduces a novel Framework called UCAFEL, which combines both Encoder and Augmentor-based methods to create a unified architecture for unsupervised feature extraction. UCAFEL uses two encoder networks that generate a compact representation and encourage the similarity between transformed data. This results in a compact and optimal representation with no need for pre-defined transformation techniques. This study also investigates a specific instance of the UCAFEL framework called the Encoder-Augmentor Autoencoder, which outperforms the existing baselines on real-world datasets. This network's simplicity and the universality of the UCAFEL framework make it a promising starting point for various Feature Extraction applications. This study also provides Python code for the UCAFEL framework. This research is relevant to fields like computer vision and natural language processing. This study also presents UCAFEL from the perspective of both encoder and data augmentation, which has not been explored before. We establish an infinite sequence of locally arc-transitive graphs characterized by a unique property: their automorphism groups partition vertices into two distinct orbits while exhibiting quasiprimativity on just one orbit, specifically within a class of twisted wreath structures. Our findings expand upon a framework initially proposed by Giudici, Li, and Praeger by providing an infinite number of examples classified under the star normal quotient twisted wreath category for locally arc-transitive graphs. Our research further includes explicit generation of the Coxeter system for an infinite sequence of group symmetries. Additionally, we provide a particular finite example exhibiting an alternative structure known as the twisted wreath configuration. Moreover, our work introduces a translation equation enabling the derivation of infinite sequences of infinite groups with a known structure, thereby linking our findings to a specific class of Foulton-Swierczowski groups. Lastly, our research includes an infinite sequence of locally arc-transitive graphs characterized by a self-complementary structure. To improve modeling long sequences in the time domain for speech separation, a dual-path RNN was previously proposed by dividing lengthy sequences into shorter chunks and processing them with internal and external RNN components. Building upon this work, a Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN) model is presented here by integrating the dual-path RNN with Convolution Recurrent Networks. The model's RNN components were substituted with dual-path modules where internal components were used to analyze single-frame spectral patterns and external components were used to analyze consecutive frame dependencies. Notably, with only 0.8 million parameters, the DPCRN model achieved an overall mean opinion score (MOS) of 3.57 in the wideband scenario of the Interspeech 2021 DNS challenge. Evaluations across additional datasets have shown the efficacy of this model. Code for the DPCRN model is available open-source on GitHub at the specified URL.

Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, mainly due to the high dimensionality of its Hilbert space. Multiple approaches have been proposed for state reconstruction, including conventional methods and machine learning applications, yet there's no universally effective protocol for deriving the Wigner function from an optical tomogram of an arbitrary light state. We demonstrate that specific non-classical effects such as the generation of entanglement and onset of quantum synchronization are directly reflected in distinct patterns of optical tomograms, eliminating the need for full state reconstruction in these instances. Our findings can be utilized in experiments where e.g. the creation of entanglement between two systems or the onset of synchronization between a pair of coupled, quantum systems results in a distinctive pattern of interference in a tomogram that signals the occurrence of these non-equilibrium, non-classical phenomena. This way, full state reconstruction can be avoided and researchers are immediately aware of the appearance of these non-equilibrium, non-classical phenomena. This approach is particularly useful when implementing state reconstruction, as it makes the process much more efficient by only requiring the measurement of a limited number of optical tomograms rather than the full set of dimensions in a quantum state. This approach is further verified through numerical simulations of two specific scenarios: the generation of entanglement in a beam splitter system and the onset of synchronization in a coupled, Kerr-like system. This is achieved by analyzing the structure of the optical tomograms in these situations and comparing them to the corresponding quantum state indicators, thereby validating the effectiveness of this approach in experimentally detecting the generation of entanglement and the onset of synchronization through optical tomograms. This method can be applied to a wide range of continuous-variable systems, as the relationship between the structure of optical tomograms and specific non-classical effects is a general principle that holds true for all systems, as long as they result in the overlap of interference patterns in optical tomograms. This method can also be combined with state reconstruction protocols, as it provides a starting point for the reconstruction process by already having measured one of the key dimensions in the Hilbert space of the quantum state. This dimension corresponds to the number of interference patterns in an optical tomogram, as defined by the relationship between the structure of optical tomograms and the corresponding quantum state. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. This allows for the model to be trained via standard knowledge distillation methods. When access to the original data isn't possible, pseudo-samples are created based on the network's decision boundaries and assigned soft labels, which serve as a transfer set for training the model. Our proposed approach is evaluated on multiple networks and datasets and shows positive results. Code is available at: https://github.com/zwang84/zsdb3kd.

Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to their scarcity. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, integrating both peer agents' knowledge and their own exploration. We validate the CoIL framework across multiple scenarios, including complex multi-agent scenarios, and observe a noticeable performance gain compared to baseline methods. As a notable aspect, peer agents do not require any initial expertise, making CoIL a practical and scalable solution for a wide range of applications. The code is available online at https://github.com/ghulghul/CoIL.

This paper proposes a metric function that yields an optimal performance when utilizing PAC codes in a Gaussian environment. Unlike previous research, the optimal performance of PAC codes isn't dependent on specific code lengths. By leveraging convex optimization techniques, the minimum distance of PAC codes can be determined for various code lengths, thereby enabling the evaluation of our proposed metric function. Our results demonstrate that using our metric function delivers performance on par with the optimal PAC codes for a range of lengths from 50 to 800. Furthermore, as the code length reaches 800, using our proposed function results in a decay rate of 2 dB in the noise margin comparison to the optimal performance. Besides this benefit, our research also uncovers the nature of PAC codes' noise margins for code lengths exceeding 800. For these longer codes, we identify specific structures that minimize the number of bits required to define the codes. As a result, we found that codes with lengths greater than 800 can be efficiently described using short polynomial arrays. This discovery enables the efficient computation of the noise margins for these codes. Moreover, we derive an analytical formula to calculate the noise margins for codes with lengths less than 800. As a special case, this formula is applied to determine the noise margin of the DPC codes commonly used in analog-to-digital converter testing applications. The proposed metric function and the derived formula agree with each other's results. As an additional contribution, we propose a new method for generating the polynomial arrays that define the codes. This generation method involves a set of linear equations that can be solved using linear algebra techniques. As a consequence, this method enables the efficient construction of the short polynomial arrays. As a special case, we apply this method to derive a specific DPC code with a noise margin of 42.18 dB. This code has a length of 800 and can be defined using a single quadratic polynomial. As another contribution, we investigate the relationship between the polynomial arrays and the codes. This investigation reveals that the codes are invariant under a set of affine transformations. As a result, we identify the equivalent codes that arise from different representations of the same code. As a consequence, we develop a new method for determining the noise margin of a code. This method involves determining the noise margin of one representative code and then applying this result to all equivalent codes. As a special case, we apply this method to derive the noise margin of a DPC code. The proposed method delivers a code that has a decay rate of 2 dB in the noise margin comparison to the optimal DPC code

Using reinforcement learning post maximum likelihood estimation pre-training can significantly improve neural machine translation efficiency. Nonetheless, a notable issue with RL for NMT arises from the large action space hindering its performance, as our hypothesis proposes. We've conducted two series of experiments which support this assumption and yield notable outcomes. Firstly, reducing the vocabulary's size enhances the RL's effectiveness, as our findings indicate. Furthermore, a notable improvement can be observed when the action space is reduced without changing the vocabulary, as validated by multiple metrics including BLEU scores, semantic similarity and human assessment. Our research discovered that initializing the final fully connected layer with a layer that generalizes action similarities resulted in substantial RL performance gains, averaging 1.5 BLEU points improvement. We believe this outcome is unique to RL and action spaces, as other experiments failed to replicate it. A straightforward, readily available code is provided to reproduce our results. We suggest several potential avenues for further research in this area. Our data and models are available at github.com/UCLA-CLAI/Small-NMT.

A rational number p/q represents the basis for a numbering system. Words composed of digits 0 through p-1 in base p/q correspond to unique rational numbers, which make up the set Np/q. Our initial contribution identifies the subsets defined by first-order logic similar to those defined by the Bachi-Bruyere Theorem in integer base systems. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that both natural order relation and modulo-q operator are not recognisable within base p/q systems. Additionally, our work introduces a method for converting finite automata in (Ap)d to (p,q) pairs, and shows that the Coale-Lindstrom conjecture holds true for a specific subset of these pairs. We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we recorded data for 12-day periods right around each encounter. These observations took place as close as 27.8 times the radius of the sun from the solar center, and we based our energy flux calculations on readings for electron density, temperature, and speed, along with the bulk characteristics of solar protons. Combining the data from the four approaches, we found the average energy flux that could reach the solar surface and counteract gravity is about 70 Watts per square meter, plus or minus 14 Watts. Notably, this is similar to the findings of other researchers using data from different spacecraft and covering a longer time period, but with a key difference being that the solar wind energy distributions were much more symmetrical and normally distributed than seen closer to the Earth, likely due to the influence of solar plasma fluctuations being limited by the close distance. Additionally, we were able to rule out any significant effects from solar nebulosity, magnetic flux tubes, or solar wind streams that had begun to form, and we concluded that the primary obstacle to receding solar surface layers is indeed the solar wind itself. With these outcomes, we believe that further analysis of the solar wind energy distributions will continue to reveal the underlying factors limiting solar surface layer recession beyond just the solar wind, such as plasma turbulence, solar wind streams, solar nebulosity, and radiation, as well as the influence of solar flux tube geometry. Moreover, we propose a method for estimating the energy flux of solar wind streams that form at greater distances from the solar surface, which could be tested using data from future close approaches. Lastly, with sufficient data from the full mission, we anticipate that the solar wind energy distributions will vary over time, allowing for a deeper understanding of solar wind and plasma dynamics, and potentially even shedding light on solar cycle-related changes. The current observations are consistent with the hypothesis that the primary obstacle to solar surface layer recession is indeed the solar wind itself, and we believe this has implications for our understanding of the solar interior and the dynamics of the solar wind, as it suggests that the solar wind energy flux that reaches the inner heliosphere is sufficient to prevent solar surface layer recession beyond a certain point, and that this point does not change over time. Thanks to speech-emotion recognition technology, computers can engage with people on a more emotional level. Nonetheless, the accuracy of speech-emotion recognition in real-world situations remains an area of improvement. A major limitation of existing methods is their inability to adapt models to new domains seamlessly. In response, researchers have developed innovative domain adaptation techniques that transfer knowledge across domains, yielding significant improvements. While these advancements are promising, there is still room for growth in adapting models to real-time, live data scenarios. A deep reinforcement learning-based strategy is presented here to adapt a pre-trained model in real-time while interacting with its environment. In evaluating the proposed approach on speech-emotion recognition tasks, the results show notable gains, with performance exceeding baseline levels by 11 and 14% in two respective scenarios. Moreover, the methodology demonstrated its practical utility in a live demonstration at the ACM Multimedia Conference. The code for this project is available open-source on GitHub.

In 2015, CERN introduced "Emittance Scans," a new fast luminosity separation scanning method at the Large Hadron Collider. These scans were consistently carried out during physics production runs, utilizing full-intensity beams at the CMS experiment's interaction point. The emittance scans allowed for the simultaneous measurement of beam properties and closed orbits at the level of individual bunches, yielding precise insights into long-range beam-beam effects, as predicted by the improved TRAIN code. The code successfully reproduced the observed beam distribution, even in the presence of significant closed-track effects, which influenced beam behavior along the ring. The code further enabled emittance to be measured along the ring, yielding a value of 3.65 ± 0.03 μm, and revealed multiple superimposed closed orbits contributing to beam scattering, which could be distinguished based on the scan's sensitivity to beam beta functions. The results validated the theoretical prediction of long-range beam-beam effects affecting beam behavior along the ring and provided empirical support for the emittance determination method used. The technique and analysis have been found suitable for other LHC interaction points, and the data obtained have been utilized to update the beam property database at the LHC. However, the signal's weakness necessitates sophisticated and highly sensitive experiments that observe the sky across various frequencies with thousands of polarisation-sensitive detectors. While such experiments with multiple detectors scanning the sky offer high-resolution data, they also produce vast amounts of data with intricate instrumental characteristics that influence the measurement process and complicate data analysis by introducing various systematic errors. To facilitate efficient data analysis, researchers focus on developing highly advanced algorithms that account for instrumental effects in the prediction of cosmic signals. To address this challenge, we present a Python tool, s4cmb, which generates synthetic cosmic signals based on realistic instrumental responses mimicking those of actual experiments. In the task of arranging unordered words into a meaningful order, prior approaches rely on using linear models to score different orderings of the same word set. In contrast, our method leverages the strong language performance following the BART framework, evaluating the coherence of orderings rather than their literal truth. We exploit BART to assess the quality of orderings, using masked filling tasks that fill the gaps between words with suitable connectors. Our analysis indicates that high-performance BART models naturally excel at this task, effortlessly achieving nearly perfect performance on artificial datasets. Moreover, we discover that using BART to evaluate orderings is particularly effective, outperforming linear models in various evaluation metrics. To demonstrate the practical utility of this approach, we integrate BART into the existing word ordering framework WordOrderNet, enabling the selection of high-quality orderings that, when connected with regular verbs, accurately predict the past tense of given words. Interestingly, our findings reveal that BART often struggles with orderings involving abstract concepts, demonstrating a limitation in its capability to perform complex tasks that require a deep understanding of the world. We conclude that pre-trained language models like BART excel at evaluating the order of words based on their semantic relationships, yet their ability to do so is bounded by their limited comprehension of the world. We make our code available at https://github.com/nyuVLabs/WordOrderBART.

The rapid dissemination of ultra-realistic media over social platforms necessitates the immediate development of an efficient and adaptable technique for identifying deepfakes. Deepfake creation methods inadvertently leave distinguishing patterns in the frequency spectra of fabricated images and videos. Leveraging this insight, our research introduces a novel detection method, known as the MD-CSDNetwork, which combines features from spatial and frequency domains to derive a unified, discriminative representation for deepfake classification. The proposed network architecture, comprising two parallel branches processing spatial and frequency information, is designed to treat multiple domain inputs as interconnected learning signals. Through cross-stitch connections between the branches, our system automatically identifies an optimal blend of domain-specific and shared features, thereby enhancing performance and generalization. Evaluations conducted on the widely-used FaceForeniscs++ benchmark demonstrate improved classification results for various manipulation types and comparable performance to state-of-the-art approaches on the Celeb-DF and Deepfake Detection Dataset. The code for this research is available open-source on GitHub.

Thousands of white-light stellar flares are now being observed through high precision, long-baseline photometry from space missions including Kepler, K2, and TESS, which provide vital information for assessing exoplanetary biosignatures and the habitability of planets in low-mass stars' UV environments. Despite this advancement, a critical limitation remains in assessing these variables, which stems from the lack of data on near-ultraviolet spectral stellar flares. As such, a grid of updated radiative-hydrodynamic simulations, which incorporates enhanced pressure broadening of hydrogen lines, is being used to predict the continuum flux of $\lambda \approx 1800-3300$ Å\  in a well-studied superflare from AD Leo during its peak phases. This prediction model utilizes semi-empirical combinations of radiative electron beam flux spectra consisting of two electron beam models: a high-flux simulation with a high energy cutoff and a lower-flux simulation with a lower energy cutoff. This two-component approach effectively explains the Balmer line broadening, the optical color temperature, the Balmer jump strength, and the far-ultraviolet continuum in the peak phases of this flare. Additionally, a comparative analysis is conducted with solar flare data, including those from the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph, which provide spatial resolution, combined with previous modeling of the SOL20140329T17:48 X1 solar flare, to demonstrate that the two-component electron beam model can be interpreted as the superposition of bright flare kernels and weaker ribbons in a larger area. This two-component model can also be seen as a continuously between these two extremes as the flare ribbons' flux and electron beam energy cutoff vary. This analysis highlights the importance of considering the distribution of heat and energy in flares when analyzing exoflare spectra. Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this, we present a novel framework called TPC that generates robust models by exposing them to transformation-based smoothing processes tailored to the types of distortions they encounter. We have tested TPC on nippet-based models and found it to significantly enhance their robustness against stretching and rotation compared to existing methods. Furthermore, TPC outperforms current benchmarks for models trained with latent codes. We have also incorporated TPC into a nippet-free point cloud classifier and demonstrated its superiority over existing robustification techniques. These findings have far-reaching implications, highlighting the significance of exploring the complex energy plane for excited states and providing a more nuanced understanding of the $^{16}$O electric dipole giant resonance. Additionally, residual interactions were found to significantly impact the widths of the components of this resonance, and density fluctuations that were initially considered negligible were discovered to be "density fluctuations of the deformed isovector monopole" rather than "deformed isovector monopole" itself.

Combined, these studies can inform management decisions with both spatial and demographic data.  However, research populations are often captured in areas with complex habitat features that can both facilitate and hinder capture efforts.  As a result, capture-recapture models may not accurately account for how animals select space when estimating population size. Our results showed that this method can effectively combine capture-recapture and resource selection models to calculate accurate population sizes even when space use is variable.  As such, this approach can be used to conduct combined capture-recapture and resource selection studies in complex, natural environments. We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate with a fixed constant factor, specifically a fraction of the logarithm of the network size, and this estimation is accurate to a large extent (up to 1 - epsilon) among the genuine nodes for any arbitrarily small positive epsilon. The algorithm runs on n nodes with the properties of being fully decentralized, low overhead, and uncomplicated in implementation. In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and rotating black holes surrounded by scalar clouds. The introduction of an adjustable damping term within the multigrid solver algorithm ensures that solutions are independent of the initial conformal factor guess. Our approach has been implemented in the Einstein Toolkit and applies to scalar field configurations, but can be extended to other matter scenarios with similar challenge settings. Our results show that this method can compete with the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition approach, with solutions converging within 10-30 conformal factor rescaling factors. The code for this research is available at https://github.com/JasonDarling/CTTK. The typical spacetime resolution for this method is around 200-300 meters, which can be improved with denser grid arrays. Recent advances in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in individuals with spinal cord injuries. Historically, these systems have focused on upper body function recovery but have given less attention to lower limb rehabilitation. Studies utilizing non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) have explored the restoration of walking ability in paraplegia but have limitations in accurately decoding more complex aspects of gait due to EEG's restricted spatial and temporal resolution. To address this challenge, researchers utilized high-resolution electrocorticogram (ECoG) recordings from the motor cortices of healthy subjects while they walked on a treadmill. The analysis revealed a high level of accuracy (99.8%) in predicting walking state and step rate information from the recorded signals over extended periods (>16 minutes). Furthermore, incorporating a Bayesian filter method led to a high correlation between predicted and actual step rates (0.934), indicating a high potential for using this BCI in the safe control of modern prosthetic devices for walking. The results presented have implications for the development of high-resolution BCIs capable of recovering more complex aspects of lower limb function in individuals with spinal cord injuries. The data and analysis have been made publicly available to facilitate further research into this area. The currently employed technology has limitations in its applicability to paralyzed subjects due to its invasive nature but offers a valuable starting point for future non-invasive interventions. The achievement of a high level of accuracy in decoding walking state and step rate information from the motor cortices using a simple machine learning approach highlights the potential for a broad range of applications in neuroscience research. In recent years, graph-based neural network methods, like graph neural networks, have effectively tackled classification and link prediction tasks by capturing complex data representations. However, most current applications rely on static graph models, which fail to account for the ever-changing connectivity structure observed in highly dynamic systems. Utilizing static models in such scenarios leads to subpar performance. In contrast, modeling temporal changes in graph structure offers a more comprehensive understanding, going beyond classification capabilities. Current approaches primarily focus on correlation-based representations, neglecting directed relationships, which are essential in numerous domains, particularly neuroscience. Our novel model, DECENNT, seeks to address this limitation by introducing a directed and dynamic graph, trained through neural network optimization, that reflects downstream classification and prediction tasks. DECENNT outperforms existing solutions in multiple tasks and provides task-specific dynamic graphs that are easily interpretable. When applied to neuroimaging data, DECENNT-generated graphs demonstrate high consistency with existing research and provide supplementary insights. Moreover, DECENNT's temporal attention mechanism identifies pivotal time periods for predictive downstream tasks from complex time series data. The code for DECENNT is available at https://github.com/yash-sonar/DECENNT.

This work utilizes the concepts from Generalized Degrees of Freedom (GDoF) analyses and extremal network theory to examine the extremal gain resulting from optimal power control in contrast to binary (on/off) power control in large interference networks, focusing on uncovering new theoretical insights. Numerical studies have shown that in many-realistic scenarios, binary power control is near optimal, however the extremal analysis indicates there are settings where the gain from optimal power control can be substantial, also offering bounds on extremal gain values from a GDoF perspective. As its primary contribution, this research precisely defines the extremal GDoF gain of optimal over binary power control as proportional to $\sqrt{K}$, where $\Theta\left(\sqrt{K}\right)$ represents the ratio, for any number $K$. It is worth noting that this gain can vary between the minimum $\lfloor \sqrt{K}\rfloor$ and the maximum $2\lfloor \sqrt{K}\rfloor$ values, depending on how the users are positioned in the network. For the sake of completeness, a related problem about binary power control in networks with multiple transmitters and receivers is also examined. Both of these models involve a large number of users.

This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained using traditional models. Our algorithm was then integrated into a simulation of complex sediment transport with thousands of particles, comparing it to the standard method that artificially lengthens collision time steps. Our results showed that artificially stretching collision time steps leads to particles being too flexible and affects the turbulence and distribution of particles, whereas our algorithm reduces computational cost to one tenth of the standard method while retaining nearly identical accuracy. Our method also allows derivation of semi-empirical equations for particle collision time based on particle size distributions, which can be useful for even faster simulations. A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump safely on soft ground by minimizing the height of its next-hop. To achieve this, we first examined the ground's dynamic response to the robot's impact and then used an optimal control approach to determine the jump height for the next-hop. This approach aimed to maximize the stability of the robot during its jump by ensuring it cleared a barrier formed by the ground's post-impact response. To apply this research to wider contexts, we generalized our method to handle obstacles in the robot's path. This project utilized an impact response model previously developed, incorporating an iterative numerical method to assess the post-impact terrain dynamics. These simulations showed that when the ground is hard, the robot returns to its initial state, while when the ground is soft, the robot experiences ground contact during its jump. These findings are consistent with real-world experiments using a one-legged hopping robot on sand. To broaden its applicability, this research was further expanded to handle varying ground slopes by incorporating an optimal control system to regulate the robot's jump. This system ensured the robot's foot struck the ground at a precise angle, even on uneven terrain. To validate this approach, real-world experiments were conducted on the robot hopping on sand at different slopes. These experiments demonstrated that the robot's foot struck the ground successfully, with minimal rebound, even on soft ground with deep post-impact depression. These results encouraged the expansion of this research to the following scenarios: robots hopping on soft ground with obstacles, on slopes with soft ground, and on terrain with soft ground and debris. These expansions required the development of sophisticated state estimation and control systems to manage the uncertain terrain dynamics during hopping. To tackle these challenges, this project integrated an inertial measurement unit with an adaptive filter state estimation method to create an accurate model of the terrain dynamics during hopping. Furthermore, this project developed a nonlinear model predictive control system using a hybrid formulation to control the robot's hop on uneven terrain with obstacles. These simulations showed that the control system managed the uncertain terrain during hopping by clearing a barrier formed by the ground's post-impact response. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content. HDTM outperformed the existing state-of-the-art method in terms of hierarchy accuracy and significantly reduced the computational requirements needed for similar results. In particular, HDTM was capable of modeling over 2 million documents with just 128MB of memory. Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system: quantum annealing delves into the equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian through gradual parameter modifications and serves as a problem-solving technique for intricate optimization problems, whereas quenching involves sudden, abrupt changes to the Hamiltonian resulting in non-equilibrium scenarios. This study investigates the interconnection between the two scenarios and reveals that the minimal point of the annealing gap, a critical obstacle in quantum annealing algorithms, can be determined from a dynamical quench parameter that defines the quantum state following the quench. When combined with statistical tools, such as neural network training, this relationship between quench and annealing dynamics can be utilized to accurately reproduce the annealing gap's functional behavior based solely on the quench data. As such, partial or full understanding of the annealing gap, obtained in this manner, can be employed to devise optimized quantum annealing protocols, leading to a tangible improvement in solution-finding efficiency. These findings stem from simulations of random Ising Hamiltonians that model complex, intractable instances of the exact cover problem. The research demonstrates that the quench dynamics and quantum annealing are intimately connected, and that the annealing gap's behavior can be deduced from the quench data, thereby providing a practical solution for overcoming one of the major challenges in quantum annealing algorithms. The study's underlying simulation framework is versatile and applicable to a broad range of problems and scenarios. Starting from a reliable two-dimensional model with two bands derived from
$d$ and $s$ orbital types for infinite layered nickelates, we investigate the
extent to which it can be reduced to a simplified one-band Hubbard model. 
Screening of the $s$-like orbital's influence is a critical factor here. 
Without screening, an isolated highly-correlated band yields an
antiferromagnetic ground state. For mild screening, strong correlations cause
the more freely moving $s$-electrons to shift to the $d$-band and the nickelate
then becomes a half-filled, highly insulating state. This case is notably
distinct from high-$T_c$ cuprates, with $s$-wave symmetry being a more
expected phenomenon. 
On the other hand, strong screening leads to a mixture of filled and weakly
coupled $s$ and $d_{x^2-y^2}$ bands and results in self-doped $d$ orbital and
$d$-wave pairing tendencies emerging. 
Interestingly, strong screening allows for another one-band physics approximation,
this time incorporating significant weight transfer when an extra filled $s$-band
is included, exhibiting both one-band physics and Kondo-lattice-like behavior,
which arises solely from this single model. 
Ultimately, our in-depth analysis highlights the intricate challenges involved
in reducing this complex two-band model to a simplified one-band model. 
Despite these difficulties, we do find one-band physics approximations that
can be utilized, depending on the level of screening. 
These approximations encompass a range of physics, from the interplay between
Kondo and lattice effects to strong correlations and $d$-wave pairing. 
These findings are all based on a non-perturbative treatment of the screening
and the correlation effects. 
We also investigate the role of finite Coulomb interactions between the $s$
and $d$ orbital screens, discovering that even at the level of screening, the
physics remains robust against this interaction. 
Our results are relevant to ongoing and planned experiments where the level of
screening can be adjusted, either through chemical means or by varying the
thickness of the sample. 
These findings open the door for adjusting the screening to deliberately
exploit the various one-band physics projections that are all based on this
single two-band model. 
In particular, we propose that strong screening could be either chemical or
geometric in nature, offering the potential for spatial variations in the
physics

The characteristics of dense matter within the density range of 1-10 times nuclear saturation density, present in compact stars, are intriguingly ambiguous and may influence neutron star dynamics as detected via gravitational waves.  As a compact star's density increases, sound velocity approaches the conformal limit at high densities, satisfying the causality limit while its detailed behavior remains disputed. It's hypothesized that dense matter sound velocity can be an indicator of a deconfinement phase transition, possibly exhibiting a distinctive relationship with density. Our work delves into the fundamental properties of dense matter sound velocity and the adiabatic index within neutron stars, quark stars, and hybrid stars.  By simulating the hadron-quark phase transition with different interface tension, we found the sound velocity's expected behavior could also arise from the quark phase's nonperturbative properties.  Consequently, this could result in a denser star with similar mass, and our calculations yield sequences for both hybrid and quark star models.  By applying this to quark stars composed of color superconducting matter, our findings indicate that sound velocity may also exhibit a distinct drop at high densities, potentially serving as a more sensitive indicator of quark matter than guassian surface gravity.  This could offer a more straightforward analysis of the MIT bag model's underlying parameters, even for more complex equations of state.  This framework is applicable to compact stars with densities 2-10 times nuclear saturation density, and our results are relevant to future gravitational wave observations, particularly those involving the most compact stars with high densities.  This could provide insights into the quark phase's nonperturbative properties and the deconfinement transition in dense matter.  Furthermore, our analysis highlights the sound velocity's predictive value in predicting quark star properties, and our predictions are based on the assumption that the quark phase's nonperturbative properties remain unchanged.  This is supported by the fact that the quark phase's surface density is minimal when the quark phase's nonperturbative properties are significant.  This could result in the surface density being undetectable in future gravitational wave observations, and the quark phase's surface density is irrelevant in the analysis of quark stars composed of color superconducting matter.  In contrast, the surface density becomes noticeable at high densities in the absence of nonperturbative properties.  During this time, the sound velocity drops significantly, and this could result in quark stars with surface densities 2-10 times nuclear saturation density

High-accuracy astronomical measurements are modeled using a relativistic framework, based on post-Newtonian theory. This approach assesses hypothetical distortions in general relativity's influence on astronomical observations. A key factor influencing these measurements is a post-Newtonian parameter, denoted by $\gamma$, which measures the gravitational impact on light deflection. Analyzing this parameter, we studied the effects of varying $\gamma$ on parallax measurements from a mission like Gaia, both mathematically and computationally. Analytical calculations of variable PPN $\gamma$'s effect on observables revealed that a change in this parameter causes a global shift in parallax measurements. This led us to develop a formula linking this shift to the satellite's position, the angle between its axis and the direction to the Sun, and the uncertainty of PPN $\gamma$. Computational simulations validated our theoretical predictions. Given current $\gamma$ estimates, we believe its impact on the Gaia parallax measurement zero point is likely minimal, under 0.2 microarcseconds. Additionally, we found that this effect varies significantly with ecliptic latitude, primarily due to the Gaia scanning pattern's asymmetry, supported by additional simulations inverting the direction of the spin axis' precession. This Gaia-based $\gamma$ determination would have a precision 10 times greater than the current most precise measurement, obtained from lunar laser ranging combined with white dwarf observations. This would also make it the most precise PPN $\gamma$ measurement derived from astrometric observations to date. Lastly, we explored the potential precision of future missions with similar designs, finding that a satellite with a longer focal length and a more comprehensive scan pattern could measure $\gamma$ with a precision a thousand times greater, achieving a precision of 0.000203 microarcseconds. This could also make it possible to detect a previously unknown variation in $\gamma$, corresponding to a variation in the Earth-Sun distance of 0.1, with a derivative approach that would allow it to be independent from solar parallax measurements. This could further enable it to vary general relativity's influence on light deflection across the sky, potentially revealing the source of this variation. This could be variations in the gravitational constant, the speed of light, the Earth-Sun distance, general relativity's $\gamma$ parameter, or alternative theories of gravity. This could be achieved by monitoring the angle of light deflection across the sky, with spatial resolution and sensitivity a thousand times greater than the current precision, across the entire celestial sphere

To effectively handle questions that require a broad range of background knowledge, it's common to incorporate external knowledge. However, utilizing limitless external knowledge often results in incorporating noisy and misleading information, posing a problem for machine-based answers. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel semantic-driven knowledge-aware question answering framework, designed to manage the injection of external knowledge with varying degrees of precision. Initially, the framework filters knowledge on the basis of a coarse understanding of the question's semantics, refining its search as necessary to ensure relevance and accuracy. The knowledge-aware approach is achieved through a combination of a semantic-aware knowledge retrieval module that incorporates structural information and prioritizes relevant knowledge. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through improved performance on the CommonsenseQA dataset, outperforming strong baselines in question answering accuracy. Moreover, the approach is found to be effective in scaling to larger knowledge graphs without a significant decrease in performance. Code for this approach is available at https://github.com/ghrua/CCQACL2023.

In the context of a Parameter Server, learning a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets, leading to slower model convergence and biases. This paper explores the application of random walk learning algorithms to tackle these issues by exploiting existing connections between nodes, as they typically require less communication with the server. A random walk is proposed where a node shares the updated model with a neighbor, with the aim of visiting more informative nodes more frequently. This goal is framed as a sleeping multi-armed bandit problem to devise an efficient node sampling strategy that generates variance-reduced gradient estimates. A novel adaptive random walk learning algorithm is introduced and proven to converge theoretically. Moreover, our results demonstrate its superior performance compared to other random walk algorithms. The proposed method is further evaluated using real-world data sets, with the results showing its applicability and effectiveness in various scenarios. We employ a 1+1+2 covariant semi-tetrad method to describe a static and spherically symmetric relativistic star comprising two fluids with anisotropic pressures, leading to the derivation of anisotropic Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations in covariant form. By direct resolution and reconstruction, new exact solutions for this two-fluid case are found. Additionally, three theorems applicable to the single-fluid scenario can be adapted to yield two-fluid solutions from their single-fluid counterparts. This approach also makes explicit the relationship between the four-velocities of the two fluids, which can be either collinear or non-collinear. Non-collinear four-velocities give rise to solutions with vorticity, providing a gravitational representation of a rotating solid body in General Relativity. A particular non-collinear scenario is presented where the two fluids share the same three-velocity and spacelike acceleration. A vast array of two-fluid solutions can be constructed using known single-fluid solutions as bases, generated through various transformations of the single-fluid solutions' parameters. These solutions encompass both isotropic and anisotropic configurations. As the two-fluid scenario allows for distinct interpretations of the two fluids, the same solution can represent either a single fluid with oscillating or rotating spacetime components, or two distinct fluids with independent four-velocity tensors. As such, it offers considerable analytical extensions to the single-fluid scenario. In contrast, little work addresses the challenge of adapting GEC to new domains with limited resources. This paper treats various GEC domains as separate tasks and proposes a novel approach, grounded in meta-learning, that achieves few-shot domain adaptation without relying on pseudo data. Leveraging rich source domains, we establish a starting point for our model's parameters that facilitates efficient adaptation on scarce resource target domains. The proposed method is applied to adapting GEC models for the native languages of second language learners. To validate our approach, we utilized nine languages as source domains and five languages as target domains in the L1 GEC domain adaptation dataset, with results showing that it outperforms the baseline multi-task transfer learning approach by a 0.50 F score on average and enables successful adaptation to new target domains with as little as 200 parallel sentences. Furthermore, by incorporating related tasks as additional source domains, we found that incorporating translation tasks as source domains can also adapt our model to new target domains, with results available in the paper. The task of allocating non-divisible goods to self-interested agents, where the valuation functions add up, and without the possibility of making monetary transactions, presents an interesting problem in fair allocation. In our investigation, we focus on whether mechanisms exist that, regardless of the situation, produce equilibria that are fair allocations for the involved agents, using only their declared, rather than true values, as input. Specifically, we are examining whether mechanisms exist for two relaxations of envy-free allocation - namely, allocating one good (EF1) or any good (EFX) fairly. Through our exploration, we investigated two established methods for achieving these relaxed envy-free allocations in a non-selfish setting: Round-Robin, known for generating allocations that are fair up to one good for any number of agents, and a cut-and-choose method of Plaut and Roughgarden, known for generating allocations that are fair up to any good for two agents. In our investigation of Round-Robin, we discovered that all equilibria resulting from it are fair allocations that are up to one good with respect to their underlying values, whereas for the Plaut and Roughgarden method, we discovered that the corresponding allocations are fair up to any good, as well as satisfying a maximin share fairness condition. Moreover, we established that for any mechanism with two agents that always has pure Nash equilibria inducing EFX allocations, this latter fairness condition holds in a weakened form. Finally, through our investigation, we established that for any mechanism with two agents that always has pure Nash equilibria inducing EF1 allocations, the corresponding allocations are fair up to one good with respect to their underlying values, whereas for any mechanism with any number of agents that always has pure Nash equilibria inducing EF1 allocations, the corresponding allocations are fair up to one good with respect to declared values. Our investigation also considered the problem of allocating one good fairly with the possibility of external consultation. In this variant, we discovered that for two agents, there exists a mechanism with pure Nash equilibria inducing allocations that are fair up to one good with respect to their underlying values, whereas for any number of agents, there exists a mechanism with pure Nash equilibria inducing allocations that are fair up to one good with respect to declared values. In our investigation, we further established that for any mechanism with two agents that always has pure Nash equilibria inducing allocations that are fair up to one good with respect to declared values, this latter fairness condition holds in a weakened form. Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among the agents' learned behavior. For example, if one agent has a random policy while the others are more skilled, existing offline methods can result in the team's performance suffering. To tackle this problem, we present a novel offline learning framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) that explicitly considers the diversity of individual trajectories. The SIT framework leverages an attention-based mechanism and a graph attention network (GAT) to prioritize high-quality experiences and encourage sharing of effective trajectories among the agents. Through rigorous evaluation, our approach achieves superior results on complex datasets, especially in scenarios with significant variations in data quality. Our code is available at https://github.com/AI-ReinforcementLearningatTexas/SIT-GAT.

In 1927, Einstein used the Solvay conference to pose a thought-provoking experiment that aimed to highlight the incompleteness of quantum mechanics. He utilized the instantaneous non-local phenomenon resulting from the collapse of a particle's wave function during measurement, famously described as'spooky action at a distance.' Prior to the influential Einstein-Podolsk-Rosen criticism of quantum mechanics' incompleteness, Einstein had already raised these concerns. We utilize the Stern-Gerlach experiment to illustrate how the instantaneous non-locality of the wave function's collapse and single-particle entanglement can give rise to the phenomenon of steering, enabling a party to influence another's quantum state based on measurement decisions made by the first party. In this process, the spreading of the entangled wave function is exploited over vast distances, demonstrating how the non-locality of single-particle entanglement allows the particle to discern the detector used by the influencing party. Consequently, despite counterarguments, our proof confirms that single-particle entanglement results in genuine non-local effects between distant locations, paving the way for its utilization in implementing truly non-local tasks. Furthermore, we propose using the spread of the entangled wave function as a means of measuring non-local distillation of single-particle entanglement. Lastly, our study highlights the relationship between single-particle entanglement, wave function non-locality, and steering, underscoring that these phenomena are inter-connected but distinct physical properties. As such, they vary in response to different situations and can even behave oppositely to each other. As an illustration, we examine how the spread of the wave function non-remains non-local even after the collapse of the wave function during measurement of the particle, demonstrating that this results in single-particle entanglement disappearing in open systems. Moreover, we explore the entropy associated with the spread of the wave function non-locality in the Stern-Gerlach experiment. In this context, the spread of the wave function is found to be analogous to the spread of a Markov chain, enabling the calculation of associated entropies. As an application, we examine the spread of the wave function in the presence of decoherence and find that it is resistant to the effects of decoherence. A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to construct codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Only the GMM is transferred to the mobile terminal, allowing it to find the most relevant codebook entry by measuring the responsibility of each GMM component to the received signal, without needing channel estimation. Feedback is transmitted as the index of the most responsible component and corresponding codebook entry, leading to enhanced performance over traditional approaches, notably in scenarios with limited pilot data transmission. Numerical analysis confirms the system's effectiveness. Moreover, by transferring only the GMM instead of codebooks, the system can handle a much larger terminal base without significant performance degradation. Code transmission efficiency can be further enhanced by transmitting only the most significant GMM component, resulting in up to 90% reduction in code transmission. Numerical evaluation proves this approach outperforms traditional codebooks in 4.5G and 5G environments. Moreover, with reduced code transmission, the proposed method can handle up to 70 more terminals per unit area in a 4.5G scenario, and up to 140 more terminals per unit area in a 5G scenario, without performance degradation. The proposed method can be applied to both single and multi-code transmission. The system's throughput enhancement in a 4.5G scenario with multi-code transmission is 12%, and in a 5G scenario with multi-code transmission is 20%. The proposed method can also be combined with other precoder codebook and feedback encoding approaches for further performance improvement. The approach has been validated with real-world data in a 4.5G scenario. We examine the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytical model for the early universe. Our framework accounts for the movement of Population III binary remnants during the formation of the universe's structure and identifies which of these remnants fall into nuclear star clusters through gravitational interaction with field stars. Following this, we track their subsequent development within these clusters through gravitational encounters and gravitational waves, and predict the likelihood of mergers of Population III binary remnants. Our study shows that about 7.5% of Population III binary remnants become situated in the centres of galaxies and 5-50% of these will merge in nuclear star clusters at high redshifts. These events peak at z=5-7 with a merger rate of 0.4-10 years^-1 Gpc^-3. Our predictions also reveal that the most massive of these remnants primarily reside in small, low-mass nuclear star clusters formed in the early universe. These clusters host black holes of masses 40-85 M_\\odot that can produce detections similar to GW190521, specifically in a mass range typically found for pulsational pair-instability supernovae with a merger rate of 0.01-0.09 years^-1 Gpc^-3. Our study highlights the importance of considering the movement of Population III binary remnants during the formation of the universe's structure and shows that nuclear star clusters at high redshifts contribute significantly to the merger rate of extremely massive black hole binaries. Our findings also support the proposal for a subclass of pulsational pair-instability supernovae based on theoretical models. Our study can be expanded to account for the movement of binary remnants during the formation of the universe's structure during its later stages. Our results align with those obtained using N-body simulations and highlight the effectiveness of our semi-analytical model. Our study provides a foundation for using the mergers of Population III binary remnants as a cosmological probe. Our results can be expanded to investigate the mergers of binary remnants formed in the early universe within the Milky Way's dwarf satellite galaxies. Our study highlights the role of nuclear star clusters in forming binary neutron star and black hole binaries in the Milky Way. Our results show that about 10% of the Milky Way's binary neutron star and black hole binaries reside in the centres of the galaxy. Our study provides a foundation for searching for these binaries in the galaxy's centre.
