In this study, we examine the security risks associated with wireless communication systems that use dual hop OFDM technology. To mitigate this issue, we analyze two main cases: one involving a single user with a single relay, and another with multiple users and relays. The primary goal of this investigation is to determine optimal power allocation methods across various frequencies in order to enhance end-to-end data transmission security while adhering to power consumption constraints at both the sender and relay nodes. By utilizing high signal-to-noise ratio approximations and optimization techniques, we can develop effective power allocation methods that prioritize system security while minimizing interference from power consumption at transmitting nodes. Furthermore, a dual decomposition framework enables us to employ convex optimization to find efficient power loading solutions. We also investigate several suboptimal schemes for various configurations and present simulation results to validate the efficacy of these methods in real-world applications. The research findings can be applied to various wireless communication systems, including cellular networks, satellite technology, and coin-cell powered wireless applications. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. 
To demonstrate its effectiveness, we saw fit to conduct a straightforward yet meaningful experiment in which we doubled the level of difficulty in three popular text-based games and observed the resulting change in performance. 
The resulting data shows that TextWorldExpress exhibits remarkable resilience, with only a 20% decline in processing speed when increasing the game's complexity by 100%. 
Our findings also highlight areas where further improvements can be made, such as optimizing memory usage. 
TextWorldExpress is available under the permissive BSD license. 
To facilitate seamless participation in ongoing research projects, we are awarding a total of $5000 to individuals who successfully complete specific challenges in TextWorldExpress. 
This initiative is part of the TextWorldExpress Challenge launched by the text game development community.

Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been highly effective in various sequence analysis tasks but suffer from limitations in their practical application due to their size. This problem is particularly pronounced in video recognition, which involves high-dimensional data. In an attempt to overcome these constraints and unlock the full potential of LSTMs, this research proposes an integrated design of algorithms and hardware to achieve high-performance, energy-efficient LSTM networks. At the algorithmic level, a new LSTM structure called FDHT-LSTM is developed, which significantly reduces model complexity without sacrificing accuracy. In addition to this optimization, a hardware platform is also specifically designed to efficiently execute the FDHT-LSTM algorithm. This custom hardware utilizes a Hierarchical Tucker Decomposition-based core memory and a highly efficient data path to minimize memory usage and increase computational speed. As a result, the energy consumption and operating frequency of the network are substantially lowered, enabling real-time recognition of high-resolution video data. Experiments conducted on a range of datasets have consistently shown that the proposed FDHT-LSTM network outperforms existing compressed LSTM networks in terms of accuracy while significantly reducing its size. Furthermore, the custom hardware provides a processing capacity that is 16 times greater than that of a high-performance GPU. In summary, this research introduces a groundbreaking algorithmic and hardware co-design framework called FDHT-LSTM, which has far-reaching implications for the practical application of LSTM models in various real-world scenarios. In particular, this network has immense potential in video recognition tasks, as evidenced by its ability to accurately recognize 640x480 video data with a relatively small model size of approximately 1.5 million transistors. In contrast, existing compressed LSTM networks require millions of transistors, making them impractical for real-world deployment. The concept of the Weak Gravity Conjecture is often expressed through its effect on the mass-to-charge ratio of a particle. Another approach posits its fundamental expression is tied to the self-repulsive properties of a specific particle in long-range interactions. A new, closely related formulation suggests it could be formulated in terms of a particle's self-binding energy, which must remain non-negative. This new interpretation becomes particularly insightful within anti-de Sitter space due to its association with a conformal field theory, where a relationship involving the dimension of an operator exists and forms a convex function of the operator's charge under a U(1) symmetry. The novelty of this formulation's structure allows it to bypass any allusion to the theory's holographic duality and spacetime locality. Consequently, it's hypothesized that the property of a convex spectrum of charges should apply broadly to all conformal field theories that are unitary. The proposed conjecture of Charge Convexity, which encompasses not just the U(1) case, can be validated by testing the property of a convex spectrum of charges across a range of models where the dimensions of operators are analytically derivable through perturbation theory, expansions in N, and semi-classical approximations. Our exploratory examination reveals that the Charge Convexity Conjecture is upheld in each instance examined, yet we have not discerned the underlying reason for this behavior from the perspective of conformal field theory. The proposed conjecture's validity can be assessed through testing the property of a convex spectrum of charges across a range of models where the dimensions of operators are analytically derivable through perturbation theory, expansions in N, and semi-classical approximations. The rapid transformation of the electricity sector necessitates innovative ancillary services that guarantee the stability and dependability of the electricity network. Unfortunately, evaluations and policy advice concerning ancillary services and market structures lack methods for examining the intricate interplay between markets and services. Consequently, this study presents an open-source agent-based model to evaluate design options for ancillary services and electricity markets. The Ancillary Services Acquisition Model integrates the MESA agent-based modeling framework with the PyPSA Python toolset for Power System Analysis. This model offers adjustable market parameters, agent-specific tactics, and thorough clearing algorithms for the day-ahead market, continuous intra-day trading, redispatch, and imbalance management. Furthermore, the model includes multiple policy performance indicators, including a novel pricing multiplier and new redispatch performance indicators. The results from a stylized simulation scenario validated the model and explored a redispatch design issue, revealing several key implications. The findings indicate that, when implementing order types in multi-period redispatch markets, the following effects are produced: the risk is minimized for market participants due to complete order fulfillment, but this may lead to increased trading of imbalances during intra-day and dispatch ramp risks, resulting from large orders; meanwhile, the grid operator over-procures redispatch during peak periods when all-or-none design is employed, which can also lead to induced imbalances due to inadequate redispatch activation. The model is available for downloading on the following webpage: https://github.com/ancillaryservices/ASAM. The ASAM repository includes the model along with sample simulation data for reproducibility purposes. The model's source code can be modified to accommodate various research applications and policy designs for ancillary services and electricity markets. The development of the model also raises several research challenges, including integration with existing models, wind turbine ramp models, order type effects on intra-day trading, induced imbalances, and redispatch supply curve estimation. The solutions to these challenges are likely to contribute significantly to the advancement of power systems research. The model's limitations are as follows: it employs a simplified market parameter setup, agent-specific tactics are required for realistic simulations, and the model lacks an estimation module for wind turbine ramp models and redispatch supply curves. The model's performance can be enhanced by integrating it with the PyPSA-Python toolset for Power System Analysis, MESA agent-based modeling framework, and the irol redispatch module. The vortex in the north was found to be surrounded by a strengthening temperature gradient at 78 degrees latitude and displayed a hexagonal shape. We demonstrate that solutions with negative energy will inevitably collapse within a finite time period. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is not too strongly energy-dependent and given specific symmetry conditions, we establish the same optimal blow-up criterion found by Holmer and Roudenko for solutions in an infinite domain. A previously established approach, derived by Glassey through the concavity of variance, is not applicable in this context due to the appearance of boundary terms of undesirable sign in the second derivative of variance. Our primary argument introduces a new, modified variance measure, bounded from below and concave in a way that is relevant for solutions in this particular scenario. It is essential to note that the approach used does not rely on the specific form of the nonlinearity, instead focusing on its general characteristics. Moreover, we provide a lower bound for the blow-up time, compared to the energy-based estimate provided by Glassey. These fractures can be viewed as interfaces within a $d$-dimensional space, where $d$ equals either $2$ or $3$. A significant distinction is drawn between fractures with notably high and low permeability compared to their surrounding medium, categorized as conductive and blocking fractures respectively. Our proposed method uses traditional hybrid-dimensional techniques to model conductive fractures and a more recent Dirac-$\delta$ function approach for blocking fractures. This results in our numerical scheme being compatible with nonconforming meshes in regards to the blocking fractures. A major advancement of our approach, the method also achieves conservative and symmetric results with regards to pressure. This methodology's effectiveness is demonstrated through the execution of numerous test cases across both two and three-dimensional settings. Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in cognitive science, where Bayes factors can compare and contrast competing theories by assessing their consistency with available data. However, implementing Bayes factor analysis is often complicated and heavily dependent on the accuracy of computational methods, as well as assumptions related to the model and data. We aim to investigate these challenges in cognitive science using Bayes factor analysis, focusing on the underlying statistical concepts and the need for objective utility functions to make informed decisions. We explore various issues with Bayes factor estimates, including their tendency to err and the reliability of bridge sampling, especially when analyzing complex scenarios. To tackle these challenges, we develop a simulation-based approach for validating the accuracy of Bayes factor estimates and examine the stability of Bayes factors in relation to different Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) draws. We also investigate the variability of Bayes factor estimates and the effectiveness of utility functions in making informed decisions. To facilitate the assessment of Bayes factor reliability, we outline a step-by-step workflow that researchers can use to evaluate the performance of Bayes factor analysis for their individual studies, including an illustrative example from the cognitive sciences. We anticipate that this research will contribute to the development of a robust methodology for evaluating scientific hypotheses based on Bayes factor analysis, along with reproducible code available online. Further discussions on the related challenges and potential solutions are also presented in the paper. Lastly, we outline potential avenues for future research and associated code development. Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on existing datasets used for this task. These predictions enable researchers to investigate the relationship between discourse indicators and the annotated semantic relations. Existing studies have established correlations between indicators and discourse relationships but are limited to specific categories and do not account for the diverse range of indicators. To address this, this work introduces the DiscSense dataset, which comprises predictions made on the existing SemRel and DiscCourse datasets along with the Discourse Markers Ontology. This new dataset showcases the diverse set of indicators associated with each semantic relation and provides a framework for classifying discourse markers. Results are presented showcasing the diversity of indicators associated with each relation and the efficacy of a simple classifier that integrates sentence representations with discourse indicators to compare against existing baselines. The research and findings presented can be used to inform the development of automatic discourse marker prediction models and provide a framework for classifying these markers. We investigate a general matrix optimization problem subject to a fixed-rank positive semidefinite constraint and perform the Burer-Monteiro factorization to analyze its landscape under a particular Riemannian quotient geometry. Assuming standard strong convexity and smoothness properties for the objective function f, we find that its factorized version exhibits distinct behaviors in three regions: (1) near the target parameter of interest, it is geodesically strongly convex and smooth; (2) it has neighborhoods of strict saddle points; and (3) it has large gradients in remaining areas. We contribute a global landscape analysis under the Riemannian quotient geometry for the first time and provide a geometric explanation for the effectiveness of vanilla gradient descent in this setting. When f satisfies a weaker convexity property, we discover a geodesically convex neighborhood around local minimizers. To achieve these results, we analyze a matrix factorization problem with a least squares objective, providing a critical connection, and also establish an independent result regarding the convexity of geodesic balls under the Riemannian quotient geometry. Finally, our work's implications are demonstrated on a matrix completion example. A graph's edge coloring can be described as assigning different colors to edges based on a specific distance criterion, with the aim of using the fewest colors possible. This concept can be taken further to a stronger standard, known as a strong edge coloring, where no two edges of the same color are adjacent to each other. Additionally, a condition known as'strongly regular' can be combined with edge coloring, resulting in a condition known as'strong edge coloring'. In this context, a bipartite graph is defined as having two distinct subgroups within its vertex set. We examined all-cubic bipartite graphs in depth and discovered that they require a specific color scheme, but it's unclear if this scheme is always the minimum required. Now, we have discovered a graph that falls into this category but uses a different number of colors. Specifically, we found an all-cubic strongly regular graph where the defined distance between vertices is two, and it uses more colors than necessary for its regular structure. This discovery serves as a counterexample to a previously proposed conjecture. We employed co-evolutionary genetic algorithms to simulate a large-scale Cournot model consisting of multiple interacting markets with symmetric players. In each market, players aimed to maximize their profit by producing optimal output levels, resulting in the emergence of a Nash Equilibrium. We examined the convergence of players' production levels to the Nash Equilibrium through genetic algorithms and identified several factors that influenced this convergence. Specifically, we found that: (1) the presence of innovation accelerated convergence to the Nash Equilibrium, (2) the degree of innovation had a linear relationship with the convergence rate, (3) smaller population sizes led to slower convergence, (4) higher mutation rates hindered convergence, and (5) the presence of noise disrupted convergence. Furthermore, we observed that the generated data could be used to simulate the dynamics of production levels in each market under the Nash Equilibrium. This research also explored the phenomenon of "lock-in" in which players became trapped in a local optimum, and we found that this occurred frequently in larger populations with lower levels of innovation. We were able to further investigate this phenomenon in a single-market setting and discovered that it could lead to markets becoming locked into a state of oligopoly rather than converging to the Nash Equilibrium. This research also examined the effects of different market parameters on the distribution of production levels and found that it was influenced by the relationship between the cost function and the number of players. We discovered that the distribution of production levels could be changed from a unimodal to a bimodal distribution when the marginal cost of production exceeded a certain threshold. This resulted in the market breaking down into two distinct groups: one consisting of small players with high profit margins and another dominated by a single large player with low profit margins. This research has implications for the study of complex systems and co-evolutionary processes, and it highlights the importance of considering noise and innovation as drivers of change and convergence in economics and sociology. This research has also led to a better understanding of the lock-in phenomenon and its effects on social and economic systems. It has also enabled the simulation of distribution of production levels in a market under the Nash Equilibrium and has shown that simple models can be used to explain complex economic phenomena. It has also highlighted the challenges and limitations of genetic algorithms in simulating systems with multiple Nash Equilibria. This research has also explored the relationship between the lock-in phenomenon and the existence of multiple Nash Equilibria in a Cournot game. We build a unified vocabulary space that spans multiple languages using the concept of distributional semantics. This approach enables seamless knowledge sharing and resource transfer between languages, extending beyond the realm of word-to-word translations. Our innovation includes aligning word clusters across languages and ensuring that the structure of these clusters remains consistent across different languages. We extract three key factors that influence clustering: neighboring words within each language's word space, character-level attributes, and linguistic patterns, which can be leveraged from knowledge bases available for over a thousand languages. We employ a novel cluster-consistent neural network to construct this unified vocabulary space by synchronizing words from different languages based on their intrinsic semantic properties. Our results show that this approach outperforms existing methods in multiple evaluations, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach for over a dozen languages. In late October 2019, violent disturbances and extensive infrastructure damage ravaged Chile's capital, particularly in Santiago. This project aims to adapt an epidemiological model previously applied to 2005's French riots to incorporate Santiago's subway layout and accurately depict the reported geographic spread of riots within the city. The existing model simulated the disorders' temporal progression with reasonable accuracy but struggled to replicate the observed distribution of unrest in Santiago. A key limitation hindering this model's effectiveness in capturing the city's rioting patterns appears to be the absence of a mechanism representing population displacement. To address this shortcoming and improve the model's predictive power, we introduce a non-local epidemiological model featuring a more comprehensive representation of population mobility and distancing behaviors. This revised model's simulations accurately replicate both the temporal and spatial characteristics of Santiago's riots in 2019. Furthermore, by analyzing the model's parameters, we gained insights into the underlying dynamics driving the unrest, including the crucial role of moderate isolation in contributing to the disorders' spread. This research also highlights the potential applications of using subway systems as a proxy for contact networks in model-based riot projections. To facilitate replication and further development, the model's source code is made available through an open-source platform. This study's findings also suggest that the onset of riots can be anticipated by monitoring changes in citizens' behavior towards each other, in addition to the usual economic and political indicators. This discovery emerged during the 2023 Chilean protests, which occurred nearly four years after the initial riots. This research's methodologies and findings are relevant to other contexts, including but not limited to, the 2023 riots in Santiago. This project's data and model are accessible via the following web address: https://github.com/rodrigogonzalez27/riots-modeling. This repository includes the model's code, as well as the necessary information for reproducing the figures and results presented in this paper. This project's findings were published in the journal Mathematical Biosciences and Engineering under the title "A non-local epidemiological model to describe social riots: spatial and temporal analysis of Chile's 2019 protests" [1]. This model's previous iteration was discussed in the journal Discrete and Continuous Dynamical Systems Series B under the title "An non-local epidemiological model of riots: describing the spatial and temporal evolution of social unrest in France in 2005" [2]. This research develops an innovative method for addressing the containment issue with enhanced regular expressions, expanding basic patterns by integrating intersection and complement operators and incorporating regular expressions over infinitely vast character sets. Unlike traditional methods for containment assessment, this algorithm acknowledges the extended features and character sets in its calculations, bypassing the necessity to translate to automata equivalents and utilizing instead a symbolic rewriting system to solve inequality problems with regular expressions. We introduce a new approach to determining containment using a combination of Brzozowski's regular expression derivatives and Antimirov's rewriting strategy, along with an expansion of Brzozowski's derivative operator that accommodates (potentially infinite) sets of recognizable characters. Furthermore, this research provides a theoretical foundation for a previously published algorithmic approach. Our method's efficacy in solving various inequality problems with regular expressions is demonstrated. Alongside this research, we also contribute an openly accessible symbolic solver tool capable of resolving inequality problems with regular expressions, offering both command-line and web-based interfaces. This solver, available at http://regsol.cs.utoronto.ca/, enables users to input inequality problems and retrieve corresponding solution explanations. Our research paper on this subject is also openly accessible at https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.4125.

Mobile agents require accurate and robust localization, and to meet this demand, Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) algorithms have been developed to estimate positions and movements using both camera and inertial sensors' data. These models, in particular the deep learning-based VIO ones, offer the potential to provide pose information without the need to craft custom algorithms. Presently, the majority of VIO models using learning techniques, often rely on recurrent models that fuse multimodal information and process signals, although they have difficulty training and efficiency limitations. This paper proposes an external memory attention learning-based VIO framework, capable of efficiently combining the data from both the camera and inertial sensors for state estimation, and we demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of this model by accurately estimating the pose in various challenging scenarios, surpassing even the traditional and current state-of-the-art VIO baselines in various scenes. Code is available at: https://github.com/ShuaiwangSheng/EMA-VIO.

Quantum mechanics relies on linear algebra, but nonlinear operators can lead to groundbreaking findings under specific conditions. In this study, we develop a new theoretical framework based on the parent Hamiltonians of the Weyl semimetal, which we call square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal, or SHOWS for short. SHOWS is characterized by both "Fermi-arc" surfaces and hinge states connecting Weyl point projections. By constructing a 3D solid-state model with honeycomb-kagome structures and double-helix layer couplings, we both theoretically and experimentally verify the exotic SHOWS state, thereby paving the way for realizing the square-root topological properties in 3D solid-state systems. With robust hinge states and extremely sensitive anisotropic transport properties, these results open up discussions on the square-root topological properties in 3D solid-state systems and provide clear guidelines for future experimental and theoretical studies. Moreover, we propose alternative structures with both experimental and theoretical realizations of the SHOWS state, offering avenues for exploring the square-root topological properties in 3D solid-state systems. Lastly, we forecast the occurrence of the SHOWS state in 2D layered materials, both theoretically and based on actual data.

This paper introduces the Federated Selective Aggregation (FedSA) challenge, a novel approach that allows the creation of a student model for a specific task by incorporating information from multiple unconnected teachers who have trained on various projects. Our focus on FedSA originates from the common obstacle encountered when attempting to exchange model data. Researchers and organizations typically invest significant resources in developing powerful neural networks but, due to data protection, cybersecurity concerns, or ownership restrictions, they cannot freely share their trained models, despite wishing to contribute to the community. To address this challenge, we propose the FedSA approach, taking it one step further as it enables a student to excel in a different task than the teachers from which it draws information. To effectively handle FedSA, we conducted comprehensive experiments using datasets that are readily available, and our findings are now available to the public full detail. Leveraging these results, we offer the FedSA-Find-Notify-Aggregate (F2N2) methodology as a practical solution to the FedSA challenge. The F2N2 framework facilitates successful model amalgamation by introducing three key elements: (1) the FedSA problem is redefined as a resource allocation issue, (2) a student model is trained using a memory-based approach, and (3) we developed a simple yet effective aggregation method. To validate our proposed approach, we conducted experiments using real-world datasets, and the results demonstrate that FedSA is both efficient and effective. This study employs terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy to analyze the local dielectric characteristics and carrier concentrations in aluminum resonators on silicon substrates, critical components of superconducting quantum processors. Utilizing a vector calibration method, we determined the terahertz permittivity near the microwave feedline and found that etched silicon exhibits higher carrier concentrations than oxide etched silicon. We further investigate methods to reduce carrier concentrations in silicon, demonstrating the utility of near-field terahertz investigations in evaluating and identifying loss channels in quantum devices. This approach can be expanded to investigate interface flaws in other qubit systems. We also introduce a terahertz sensitivity enhancement technique using a microbolometer, which can detect the diminished terahertz permittivity of silicon due to etching. This approach enables non-contact inspections, facilitating the development of terahertz sensors for quantum devices and allowing for etching depth to be calculated from terahertz data. This technique can be applied to evaluate the material flaws in qubit systems, such as diamond and silicon qubits. This research highlights the significance of terahertz characterization in identifying and analyzing the dielectric environments of quantum devices, thereby providing crucial insights for the development of practical quantum computing. This approach can be expanded to investigate interface flaws in other qubit systems. We also discuss the implications of our findings for nanomechanical resonator quantum computing and provide a framework for near-field terahertz investigations in this context. This research paves the way for terahertz near-field microscopy to excel in identifying the flaws in quantum devices, facilitating progress in quantum computing, with the potential to expand to other qubit systems. This study is also relevant to various technological applications, including advanced sensor and bolometer technologies. This work explores the long-term evolution of Venus's atmosphere, examining how its composition has been shaped by interior-exterior interactions over time. Despite significant ongoing research, key aspects of the atmosphere's formation and current state remain unclear and require interdisciplinary analysis. We examine various processes that have influenced the atmosphere's evolution, starting with volatile sources and examining interactions from the planet's core to its upper atmosphere, as well as atmospheric escape mechanisms. We also delve into the complex historical events that have contributed to the atmosphere's evolution, including the effects of impacts, magnetic field generation, and geochemical and geodynamic feedback cycles. We then outline plausible pathways for the planet's evolution, ranging from its accretion phase to its present state, using modeling and observations. These scenarios include atmospheric escape during the magma ocean phase, prolonged surface liquid water that eventually gave way to a runaway greenhouse phase, and water retained within the planet due to inefficient outgassing, leading to hydrogen entrapment in the core and mantle oxidation. We review the existing evidence and discuss the need for future research, as well as potential observations and missions required to better understand Venus's complex interior, surface, and atmospheric interactions and how they have influenced the planet's evolution and future. This work is intended as a starting point for the broader research community, with the goal of advancing our understanding of Venus's atmosphere and advising on suitable missions to study this phenomenon further. As high-power laser pulse capabilities increase, there's a growing need for effective pulse purification to prevent damage during experiments.  A potential approach involves using magnetized plasmas to modify and enhance laser pulses, taking advantage of their nonlinear interaction properties. Through particle-in-cell simulations, we investigated the interaction between a high-power laser pulse and a relativistically charged electron bunch within a plasma filled with magnetic fields. Our findings show that dense plasmas with strong magnetic fields can increase laser pulse intensity by 100-fold and modify pulse polarization, potentially allowing a single laser system to deliver multiple polarization outputs for various applications. Furthermore, we discovered that the process is relatively robust, enabling intense pulse generation across a wide range of distances from the plasma surface. Our results suggest that magnetized plasmas can serve as compact, all-optical devices capable of transforming and amplifying laser pulses to meet diverse experimental demands. This includes next-generation particle acceleration and fusion experiments that require millions of degrees Celsius in a matter of femtoseconds. This finding has the potential to expand the functional capabilities of laser systems and enhance existing facilities without requiring significant upgrades. This research has implications for the design of plasma-based devices using magnetic fields and offers insights into the behavior of high-power laser pulses within plasmas, providing a foundation for developing more sophisticated models that incorporate both classical and quantum plasma interactions. This discovery can be experimentally verified using existing laser systems and may lead to the development of more sophisticated models incorporating quantum plasma interactions. This finding paves the way for the creation of all-optical devices using plasmas that can enhance the capabilities of existing laser systems without the need for significant upgrades. We investigate decoding of rank metric codes under the assumption of a symmetric error matrix. Our analysis yields two main conclusions. Firstly, we show that for code rates less than half, there is a diverse class of rank metric codes capable of accurately decoding any symmetric error, even those of maximal rank. Moreover, this code class includes, as a subset, the family of Gabidulin codes with rates less than half. Secondly, we propose a method for correcting symmetric errors of up to n-k rank, which can be applied for code rates greater than half. Both of these decoding strategies are deterministic and provide guaranteed performance in the worst-case scenario. In addition, we compare their performance to their corresponding list decoding counterparts under the condition of a symmetric error environment. Our findings are accompanied by relevant numerical examples to demonstrate the applicability of these decoding methods. In particular, we highlight the scenario in which one can achieve error correction up to half rates for list decoding. To greatly decrease the number of image sensors required in wide-field X-ray monitors employing lobster-eye (LE) optics, we propose a concept called multiplexed lobster-eye (MuLE) optics. This configuration involves dividing an LE mirror into multiple sections and using each one to direct X-rays onto a single shared image sensor. If each LE section is positioned at a different rotation angle, the optical system can determine the exact section responsible for focusing X-rays on the sensor. A simulation showed that the proposed MuLE arrangement consisting of 9 segments can effectively detect a signal with an energy of ~10^-10 erg cm^-2 s^-1. Furthermore, this concept permits the use of large-format image sensors that support high-time-resolution observations with comparable aperture sizes to traditional wide-field monitors. To realize this idea, we suggest using a combination of 3D printed LE mirrors and a custom-made data acquisition system. This concept has the potential to significantly reduce the cost and size of wide-field X-ray monitors. To validate this idea, we intend to build a prototype MuLE setup and conduct experiments to compare its performance with the results of our simulations. This concept can also be applied to other types of optics that disseminate light over a wide area. We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of assigning unique properties to each fluid element. This includes individual masses, specific angular momentum, and entropy levels. 

As a key departure from earlier methodologies, the angular velocity distribution within each fluid element is instead determined after the positions of all elements are calculated, allowing for more nuanced configurations. This method involves solving a vast set of nonlinear algebraic equations derived from time-independent versions of the Euler and Einstein equations, solved through our new multi-dimensional root-finding algorithm, the W4 method. 

We have successfully demonstrated our approach by generating equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under both barotropic and baroclinic conditions, and have also used this method to simulate evolutionary processes like stellar cooling, mass loss, and mass accretion, serving as basic models. These simulations aimed to track changes in the masses and compositions of stars over time. 

Notable findings from this research include evidence that low-mass rotating stars experience through a static instability before undergoing radial contraction, and that this effect can delay their cooling rates due to increased core contraction, and even causing core dimpling in low-metallicity stars. Additionally, we have also analyzed the impact of core convection on the distribution of angular velocity, and found that its effect is more pronounced in intermediate mass stars with iron core convection. 

In the process of developing this approach, we encountered several challenges and gained valuable insights into the physics of rotating stars, particularly with regards to core convection, and the effects of secular instabilities and mass accretion on stellar evolution. These discoveries have been presented in a series of companion papers.

Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their dense matter state. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the rapid identification of signals from gravitational waves in real-time. Traditional approaches struggle to achieve this at the rate expected for future detectors. The network's effectiveness is showcased in its capacity to differentiate between all types of merging compact binaries, distinguishing them from background noise. With approximately 500,000 training samples, we successfully trained a network that can recover known neutron star and binary neutron star events, and accurately classify a vast majority of candidate black hole binary merger events. These achievements are critical milestones in achieving the low-latency detection required for multi-messenger astronomy. However, COVID-19-related mobility restrictions significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, prompting concerns about their lasting social effects. The prevalence of false news is not a new issue but one that is expanding at a rapid pace. Social media has fueled the spread of misinformation by offering convenient access, coupled with limited fact-checking mechanisms. Given the negative consequences of this type of information on society, pinpointing false news has become increasingly vital. We propose an innovative method that leverages transformer-based language models to counter one of their inherent drawbacks, allowing our CMTR-BERT framework to combine diverse text representations, mitigate the sequential constraints inherent to the underlying architecture, and integrate contextual information effectively. Experimental evaluations using two disparate, publicly available datasets showcase our method's capability to achieve superior performance benchmarks, highlighting the benefits of both utilizing automatic text summarization and incorporating contextual information for enhanced performance. Moreover, our findings demonstrate the versatility of our method, as it delivers promising results with multiple diverse baselines, paving the way for its potential application across a range of natural language processing tasks beyond fake news detection. The code for this project is available at https://github.com/ghulamabidkhan/CMTR-BERT.

Traditionally, annotated data have served as inputs for supervised machine learning models. Yet, contemporary language models possess knowledge that can be leveraged to enhance annotated data. In this work, we employ BERT to fine-tune the annotation of a game-based interaction dataset called EMO20Q. Emojojoy and Emojosad, two emotional annotation categories, were assessed to determine the effectiveness of BERT. Our evaluation reveals that BERT exhibits a moderate to strong correlation of 0.43-0.58 with human annotations. Moreover, BERT-annotated data were found to be comparable to human annotations based on two metrics. Furthermore, eliminating BERT's annotations resulted in only a minor decline in performance, indicating only limited dependence on BERT. Our approach is deemed suitable for unannotated domains where novel annotations can be obtained using BERT. Additionally, we propose a hybrid annotation method that integrates BERT and human annotations. This method's efficacy is demonstrated across two evaluation metrics. By leveraging BERT to annotate unexplored emotional data, our research paves the way for extending contextualized annotation techniques to unannotated domains. Our annotated EMO20Q dataset is available for download at https://github.com/ghrua/EMO20Q_BERT.

For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting and produce a unified global map for navigation. Unfortunately, implementing these systems on a large scale can be challenging due to their tendency to deviate and slow build-up times. In response to these limitations, a novel map representation called HiTMap is presented, featuring a unique hierarchical structure that focuses solely on a local metric map for obstacle avoidance while keeping the representation lightweight. Furthermore, HiTMap detects frontiers, integrating them into the map as an attribute to guide navigation, and includes a path-planning module to evaluate the representation's feasibility and efficiency. The system's performance was validated through simulation testing and a real-world demonstration, and its source code is available openly for public use. In terms of navigation map representations, HiTMap's innovative structure makes it a valuable contribution, and the system's ability to balance mapping and navigation efficiently further differentiates it from the field. In its current form, HiTMap is suited for application on small-scale frontiers but requires extension to handle large-scale environments. Nevertheless, the approach's modular design allows for HiTMap's integration into existing mapping systems, and possible enlargement could be explored through future research and development. Experimental data related to HiTMap can be found at https://hiadm.github.io/hitmap/.

High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAr CUDA framework specifically tailored for SMMO applications.  This framework includes a dynamic memory allocator that is both lock-free and parallel, a data layout domain-specific language (DSL), and a do-all operation that is both parallel and efficient.  As a result, DynaSOAr offers improved memory usage, reduced fragmentation, and superior performance to leading state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators by concurrently managing both memory allocation and memory access through atomic operations.  Furthermore, DynaSOAr's approach allows for significant speedup and memory management efficiency gains, as demonstrated in our benchmark results, where it achieves application code performance improvements of up to 3 times and supports larger problem sizes of up to 2 times with the same memory.  As evidence of its practical utility, we successfully utilized DynaSOAr to accelerate multiple real-world object-oriented applications on the GPU.  Our findings also inform a set of programming guidelines for efficient GPU object-oriented programming.  Finally, we open-source DynaSOAr to facilitate further research and GPU programming for a broader range of object-oriented applications.

We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2.  To accurately simulate these properties, we utilized a 48-atom supercell through the VASP code, relaxing both atomic positions and cell dimensions to minimize errors. The results indicate that substitutional carbon and nitrogen defects have a tendency for anti-ferromagnetic long-range ordering with corresponding magnetic moments of 2$\mu B$ and 1$\mu B$ for carbon and nitrogen respectively.  Conversely, nitrogen defects positioned interstitially possess a fixed magnetic moment of 1$\mu B$ whereas carbon defects positioned interstitially display no magnetism.  Moreover, calculations demonstrate that interstitial N defects lie at a saddle point in the total energy landscape, and that a more stable configuration is reached when these atoms bond with oxygen in a CO or NO dimer.  Notably, this outcome is consistent with earlier experimental findings utilizing XPS that also identified such N-O bonds, and could potentially be verified via spectroscopic techniques.  Moreover, both doped carbon and nitrogen defects reside within the band gap of TiO2.  We propose that tuning TiO2 by introducing such defects could enhance its photocatalytic properties. This letter describes the inspiration and an analytical method for detecting the production of top-quark pairs in the Large Hadron Collider through the identification of protons emitted at the front end. I demonstrate the feasibility of identifying the semi-elastic process using a dataset of 300 inverse picobarns of data, and the fully elastic process appears inaccessible. Furthermore, I illustrate that utilizing forward proton tags enables limits on certain rare top-quark decays such as $t\rightarrow u\gamma$ and $t\rightarrow c\gamma$ which would significantly surpass the current world records, with limits on branching ratios of $<0.39\cdot10^{-5}$ and $<0.97\cdot10^{-5}$, respectively. The elastic potential at the Large Hadron Collider with a luminosity of 100 inverse picobarns in the forward proton tag mode exhibits promising characteristics, offering multiple physics opportunities that can be explored with existing hardware. Consequently, I propose and endorse this idea for consideration in upcoming runs with increased luminosity. The proposed analysis employs the ATLAS detector software with modifications to handle large datasets efficiently. I outline an alternative method using neural networks which can achieve the same results but with a more complex setup. Lastly, I discuss and provide estimates for detecting the semi- and fully elastic processes at the Large Hadron Collider with luminosities exceeding 300 inverse picobarns, as well as identifying the rare decays $t\rightarrow u\gamma$ and $t\rightarrow c\gamma$ at the Future Circular Hadron Collider.

Given a finite group G and a subset S of G's generating elements, the smallest possible diameter is defined as the minimum number n, such that any element of G can be expressed as the product of up to n elements from S. This research focuses on characterizing groups with a diameter that scales polynomially for a fixed-sized generating set, and it demonstrates that these groups have a significant abelian subgroup close to their highest order, making up a substantial fraction of the group's total size. This finding reinforces an important result established by Breuillard and Tointon and implies that groups with a polynomial diameter contain multiple conjugacy classes and a large nilpotent subgroup with a maximum class of two. Furthermore, it shows that the diameter of a group that is not highly solvable can be conservatively bounded by the square of its largest element size. This work also examines the relationship between a group's diameter and the scale of its largest elementary abelian subgroup components and provides explicit bounds for specific group types. This research further includes an analytical formula to calculate the diameter of a p-group generated through a set of p-element generators. This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature readings into two corresponding biasing currents, which in turn influence two distinct oscillation frequencies in direct proportion to the absolute temperature. The resulting digital temperature value is obtained by converting the frequency ratio in the sensor module's digital backend. With a simple and efficient design, the temperature sensor offers a minimal footprint, extremely low power consumption, and accurate temperature readings over a broad temperature range. Moreover, the design includes a straightforward voltage regulation mechanism, enabling it to accommodate dynamic voltage scaling. The proposed design was implemented in a 180nm CMOS process, featuring a -100{\deg}C to 0{\deg}C temperature range, a wide supply voltage range from 0.6V to 1.8V, and an incredibly compact silicon area of 0.021$mm^2$. Experimental results from 20 test chips revealed outstanding performance characteristics, including a 0.24{\deg}C resolution, a 1.4{\deg}C maximum inaccuracy, a 1.5kHz sampling rate, and an energy per conversion of 1.06nJ at 30{\deg}C. The temperature sensor was further integrated into a working 8-bit RISC processor to evaluate its performance in real-world applications, resulting in accurate temperature readings even in the presence of process, voltage, and temperature fluctuations. The test processor, comprising 7000 transistors including the temperature sensor, was implemented in the same 180nm CMOS process, allowing it to operate across a wide temperature range with minimal power consumption. The resulting performance characteristics per transistor are a 0.24{\deg}C resolution, a 1.4{\deg}C maximum inaccuracy, a 1.5kHz sampling rate, and an energy per conversion of 1.56nJ at 30{\deg}C. The proposed design presents multiple innovative features, including a compact footprint, low power consumption, and precise temperature monitoring, making it an ideal choice for complex systems that employ dynamic voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module alone can be fabricated in the 180nm CMOS process for a cost of $12, the test processor can be fabricated in the 180nm CMOS process for a cost of $21, and the theoretical area per conversion is 0.0006$mm^2$.

In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks. Code is available at github.com/songzhai/look-ahead-attention.

A unified dark fluid model has been developed that combines the characteristics of dark energy and dark matter through the use of a variable decay constant. This model has been tested and validated through the analysis of astronomical data, including supernova observations, cosmic microwave background radiation, and the absorption spectra of quasars. By applying the model to these sources of data, we have calculated its key parameters and found them to be consistent with each other. A key feature of the model is that it predicts that the distribution of galaxy rotations will deviate from the standard Hubble law due to the presence of a decaying component. Furthermore, we have calculated the decay constant's current rate of change to be approximately 0.81 x 10^-3, and we have identified several potential sources of data that will aid in further refinements of the model. Additionally, we have explored the model's implications for the cosmos and have found that it is stable and has evolved through a series of transformations from a state similar to that of the Neumann boundary layer to the current unified dark fluid era. Lastly, we have compared our model to existing dark energy and unified dark energy models, and we have discovered that it differs from them due to the variable decay constant's effect on the model's behavior. Consequently, we have determined that this model offers a more comprehensive and nuanced understanding of the cosmos and provides a promising foundation for the development of future unified models. Lastly, we have made the model available on the website "https://rbk.uni-so.ccu.ru/" for the benefit of fellow scientists.

Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of MFSSA through comparative studies of reconstruction accuracy in multivariate functional time series (MFTS) and real-world applications, including the analysis of intraday temperature curves and remote sensing images of vegetation. Additionally, MFSSA is made available through the Rfssa R package for user convenience.

The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and 0.4 meter diameter provides plasma necessary for the experiment, and features a helical antenna to produce high-density plasma in the helicon mode of discharge. Until now, it was unclear if this plasma source could achieve helicon mode, which is essential for it to function effectively. A study was conducted to verify this capability, involving detailed analysis of plasma parameters and particle power balance using a global model. It was confirmed that helicon mode exists at lower magnetic fields, and to optimize the source for maximum plasma density, it was modified to function in this mode at the highest magnetic field available. This achieved a plasma density of up to 1.6 times 10 to the 10th power electrons per cubic centimeter. Furthermore, it was discovered that helicon mode has a distinctive characteristic, namely that the cross-field plasma density becomes uniform only when the helical antenna's windings are fully ionized. To ensure reliable operation in various experiments, it was necessary to develop more robust control systems for plasma density and magnetic field. This was accomplished using feedback loops from density measurements and a magnetic field scanner. Now, the source can produce plasma with a uniform density of up to 1.6 times 10 to the 10th power electrons per cubic centimeter within a 0.2 meter radius and 0.25 meter length, and it has been confirmed that it operates in the helicon mode with excellent agreement between experimental data and global modeling results. This has paved the way for using the IShTAR facility to study interacting plasma and radio frequency waves in a controlled environment. This achievement is also expected to benefit other similar plasma sources, such as those used in material processing and medical applications. This work was published in the Plasma Sources Science and Technology journal.

While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which has yielded notable improvements in model performance. However, these methods require the manual annotation of images by experienced pathologists, thus increasing the workload. To make cancer diagnosis more efficient, it's crucial to develop a fully automatic nucleus detection algorithm capable of accurately locating and extracting valuable information from images with minimal manual intervention. In response to these challenges, this paper presents a novel approach, a W-shaped network, that automates nucleus detection in pathology images. In contrast to conventional U-Net based models, which focus directly on mapping images to their target masks, this approach divides the detection task into two distinct sub-tasks: first mapping images to binary masks, followed by transforming these masks into density masks. By breaking the detection task down in this way, the model's difficulty is substantially reduced, resulting in improved performance. Moreover, this method can be applied to other image segmentation applications beyond cancer research. To validate the effectiveness of this approach, experiments were conducted using publicly available datasets, which showed that the W-shaped network outperforms existing models in terms of accuracy. Furthermore, by applying different thresholding techniques to the models' output, this approach can not only detect isolated nuclei but also extract fused nuclei, thus providing a more comprehensive set of features that can be used in cancer research. We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games at the individual state level, and a comprehensive aggregated game representing the overall grid structure. Each of these components can be efficiently solved for a Nash equilibrium. We connect the two levels by utilizing the outcome values of the individual games as rewards in the aggregated framework. Through extensive simulations, our hierarchical model demonstrates substantial computational efficiency improvements while achieving comparable performance to flat Nash policies. Moreover, by incorporating external observation costs, our method can be applied to tackle challenging scenarios such as evading in partially observed environments. Code for this research is available at https://github.com/PranavTiwary/HierarchicalPEG.

The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The screens' velocities were found to be similar to those of nearby stars, suggesting they reside within the local interstellar medium. The distribution and characteristics of the screens also reflect the structure of the local interstellar medium, with a prominent screen aligned with the Sun-Proxima Centauri line, and another screen located at a right ascension of approximately 113.7 degrees. The study highlights the value of long-term pulsar monitoring data for uncovering the screens of the interstellar medium and the inherent variability of the local screen structures. The derived screen properties are also comparable to those found in the solar neighborhood, with a predicted screen density of approximately 10 screens per parsec squared. The study's results further emphasize the necessity for high-cadence, long-duration pulsar scintillation observations to fully explore the interstellar medium. The data analyzed in this study are available in the appendix. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of PDCNNs for unseen frequency inputs and the cascaded structure's performance in speech synthesis. Code for this research is available at: https://github.com/ParandDarabi/Quasi-Periodic-WaveNet.

Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the object generating the sound, to significantly enhance sound source localization performance. To accomplish this efficiently, we develop a method that automatically extracts challenging samples and incorporates them into a contrastive learning framework. Our algorithm achieves superior results on the Flickr SoundNet dataset, a prominent benchmark. Moreover, we introduce a new dataset called VGG-Sound Source, a comprehensive set of annotated video clips featuring sound sources with explicit bounding box markings. VGG-Sound Source surpasses existing datasets in scale, size, and category diversity, consisting of 5,000 videos spanning over 200 categories. Notably, it differs from Flickr SoundNet in that it is based on video data. Our algorithm also demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on this new dataset when compared to several baseline methods. All models are publicly available on the GitHub platform. Moreover, we present detailed implementation guidelines to facilitate replication of our results. The VGG-Sound Source dataset is available for public use. Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent across various hyperbolic geometries. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and it is particularly effective at representing tree-likeness graphs with reduced distortion. LGCN's simplicity and flexibility also enable it to be easily integrated into existing hyperbolic GCN architectures, and it can handle large graphs efficiently due to its scalable design. This is achieved by introducing a hyperbolic multi-classification layer that significantly reduces the network's complexity from an exponential to a linear relationship. This is further demonstrated by implementing LGCN in a hierarchical clustering scenario on one real-world dataset. The code for LGCN is available at https://github.com/ShuaiNiu93/LGCN.

We employ exact diagonalization to examine the effects of spin-orbit coupling and electron-electron interactions on the mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ $d$-orbital states in a cubic crystal structure, characteristic of transition metal oxides. By directly comparing with $t_{2g}$ only or $e_g$ only models based on electron filling, we investigate the magnetic properties of all possible $d$-shell configurations, incorporating calculations of the total magnetic moment, orbital occupation, and effective spin-orbit coupling. The resulting parameters are expressed in terms of interaction strength, spin-orbit coupling, and crystal field splitting within relevant 4d and 5d transition metal oxide ranges. Through various limits, our perturbative and numerical results converge, highlighting that $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing can be significant, with up to 20% orbital occupation outside nominal ranges. These findings hold important implications for experimental interpretation and can influence the theoretical models used to analyze magnetic properties and phases in these materials, where intermediate electron-electron coupling commonly prevails. Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the healthcare field. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Our research utilized the CheXpert dataset to train a StyleGAN that effectively produces authentic chest X-rays. By incorporating an encoder from the Cyclic Reverse Generator framework, we successfully developed an inverse mapping system to recreate synthetic X-rays accurately and reconstruct organs on real X-rays. By fine-tuning latent codes, we successfully transplanted a cardiac enlargement condition onto normal chest X-rays with remarkable success. Our findings were quantitatively assessed and compared to state-of-the-art unsupervised medical image editing techniques. Our findings suggest that this method outperforms existing techniques in terms of both subjective and objective evaluation measures. The trained model's capacity to reproduce authentic X-rays was validated through a generative adversarial liability test. The availability of pre-trained models can be accessed at https://github.com/gharsali-dl/DiseaseAwareEditing. With over 5 million trainable parameters, this model's potential in various medical imaging applications is substantial, as evident from the results presented. Our research opened the door for numerous possible modifications and expansions, as we deliberately kept the model's complexity minimal in order to facilitate easy modification. Our data and model codes have been uploaded to GitHub at https://github.com/gharsali-dl/DiseaseAwareEditing.
